list.shortDescription: An Indonesian savory fish cracker from southern Sumatra, made with wahoo or Spanish mackerel, tapioca starch, and other flavorings, then sun-dried and grilled or fried.

cover.altText: Kemplang: Grilled fish crackers, Bandar Lampung, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: A Kerala beef dish slow-roasted with spices, onions, curry leaves, and coconut slivers, then fried in coconut oil. In Kerala, it is also called Beef Ularthiyathu.

cover.altText: Kerala beef fry: kerala Beef fry, also known as Beef Ularthiyathu

list.shortDescription: An Algerian semolina bread cooked on a flat grilling tajine over high heat. It can be eaten hot or cold with olive oil, cheese, tajine, fermented milk (leben), or curdled milk (raib).

cover.altText: Kesra, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian vegetarian dish from Jakarta combining tofu, vegetables, rice cake, and rice vermicelli with peanut sauce.

cover.altText: Ketoprak: Ketoprak di Jakarta

list.shortDescription: A Thai dessert of small steamed cakes made with toddy palm sugar and coconut milk, wrapped in banana leaves and topped with grated coconut. It is common in sugar-palm-growing provinces such as Phetchaburi, Nakhon Pathom, and Suphanburi.

cover.altText: Khanom tan: ขนมตาล

list.shortDescription: A Thai dessert made with rice flour, coconut milk, and sugar, cooked and served in small ceramic cups known as thuai talai. Salt, eggs, and pandan essence may also be added.

cover.altText: Khanom thuai: A pair of khanom thuai talai , a Thai sweet/dessert

list.shortDescription: A Thai rice-and-curry meal pairing steamed rice with assorted curries, fried foods, and vegetables. Its rich, spicy curries make it a quick staple found in restaurants, food stalls, and markets.

cover.altText: Khao kaeng: Typical Thai Food in Street-cusine. Bangkok

list.shortDescription: A Thai adaptation of Chinese char siew: steamed rice topped with red pork, kun chiang, half-boiled duck or spiced corned eggs, and crispy fried streaky pork, covered in sweet bean gravy with cucumber and green shallots.

cover.altText: Khao mu daeng, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Filipino glutinous rice casserole whose Hokkien name means “salty rice.” Meat and Chinese sausages are cooked in an adobo-like sauce, then mixed with rice and vegetables such as taro, and topped with toasted nuts and scallions.

cover.altText: Kiampong, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A sour Kerala dish made with curd, ground cumin paste, and cucumber, ash gourd, or white gourd, garnished with sautéed mustard seeds and curry leaves. Often served as part of a Sadhya.

cover.altText: Kichadi, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A sweet prepared for Christmas as part of Kuswar in Goa and Mangalore, and also among the East Indian community of Maharashtra.

cover.altText: Kidyo: Kolkola or Kulkuls, a Goan Christmas sweet

list.shortDescription: A Ugandan dish of cut-up chapati and fried beans, created in the early 2000s as a rolex variant. Variations include avocado, meat stew, gravy, chicken, or liver.

cover.altText: Kikomando: This is an image of food from

list.shortDescription: An Angolan meat dish of roasted goat rubbed with garlic and lemon juice, with white wine, bay leaves, olive oil, and salt.
A Malagasy sweet of ground peanuts, brown sugar, and rice flour, traditional especially in the highlands. Koba akondro is wrapped in banana leaves, then steamed or boiled until the batter sets.

cover.altText: Koba: Koba (kobindravina), a dessert or snack eaten in the highlands of Madagascar, made from peanuts, brown sugar and rice flour

list.shortDescription: A South African Cape Malay pastry of yeast dough flavoured with cinnamon, aniseed, ginger, cardamom and dried tangerine peel, deep-fried, briefly cooked in syrup and rolled in coconut.

cover.altText: Koe'sister: A Koe'sister, a traditional Cape Malays pastry from Cape Town, South Africa

list.shortDescription: A Cameroonian cake of black-eyed peas or cowpeas cooked with palm oil and traditionally eaten with plantains, associated with the Mbo, Bazou, Bafang, Makaa, Bassa, and Banen peoples.

cover.altText: Koki: Koki banane poyo - Bandrefam-Cameroun

list.shortDescription: A spicy rice-based dish from Kolkata in West Bengal, shaped by Mughlai cuisine and made with meat, eggs, potatoes and spices. It is especially known for its potatoes and light blend of spices.

cover.altText: Kolkata biryani: Kolkata Biryani with two pieces of mutton (goat meat), an egg and a potato

list.shortDescription: A very salty bun eaten in Trabzon, Turkey, made with flour, salt and oil from seven houses, water from seven rivers, and seven pieces of wood from seven hedges. Folklore links eating it with dreams of possible husbands.

Kondreh is a Cameroonian dish of the Bamileke people in the West Region, especially Bafang, and is considered a national dish. It is often served at ceremonies, weddings, and funerals as a symbol of hospitality and respect.

cover.altText: Kondreh (food): Préparation de Kondre plat traditionnel camerounais avec viande de chèvre

list.shortDescription: A Korean dish of white or brown rice cooked with one or more varieties of soybeans, usually black soybeans, either combined from dried grains or prepared from scratch.

cover.altText: Kongbap: Korean cuisine-Kongbap

list.shortDescription: A Japanese seafood dish of salted, fermented sea cucumber intestines, one of the country’s chinmi. Cleaned intestines are mixed with over 10% salt by weight and are ready to eat in two to three days.

cover.altText: Konowata: このわた 春風萬里

list.shortDescription: A Makassarese rib soup from South Sulawesi, Indonesia, made with beef or spareribs in a dark, spicy broth flavored with coriander, keluwak, nutmeg, turmeric, galangal, cinnamon, tamarind, lemongrass, cloves, and salam.

cover.altText: Konro Soup: Sup Konro.Beef ribs soup of Makassar, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: A salty, spicy Greek PDO cheese from the Cyclades, produced in Mykonos for more than 300 years. Repeated kneading during ripening encourages microbial growth, rapid lipolysis and proteolysis that give it a peppery taste.

cover.altText: Kopanisti mykonou: Kopanisti, a spicy cheese made in the Cyclades, with Protected Designation of Origin

list.shortDescription: A Japanese steamed confection of rice flour, sugar, and azuki beans, with the beans kneaded directly into the dough. Common in Kyushu, especially Kagoshima Prefecture, it is usually shaped into sticks or rectangular blocks.

A Korean goat soup made with Korean Native goats, the country’s only indigenous goat breed, often containing perilla seeds, soybean paste, red pepper paste, mushrooms, leeks, cabbage, or perilla leaves.
A Javanese spicy stew of cattle skin from Yogyakarta and Central Java, Indonesia, traditionally using soft inner hide but now commonly made with rambak or krupuk kulit.

cover.altText: Krecek: Krecek atau Kerecek, Yogyakarta

list.shortDescription: Hard, coin-sized speculaas confections shaped like flattened hemispheres, traditionally linked to Sinterklaas festivities and commonly eaten in Belgium and the Netherlands.

cover.altText: Kruidnoten: Knapperige kruidnoten AH

list.shortDescription: A dry Indonesian snack from Cirebon, West Java, made with tapioca flour and grilled between iron molds like a waffle. It comes in a variety of shapes and flavors.

cover.altText: Kue gapit: Panda-brand kue gapit, a kind of cracker from Cirebon. It is made by pressing the dough in between two metal molds. These crackers are firm and crispy. The scale shows 1 cm (top) and 1 inch (bottom)

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian Betawi string-hopper dish made with starch or rice flour and coconut milk, shaped like noodles and served with kinca, chutney, or curry.

cover.altText: Kue putu mayang: Putu Mayang, sweets made of rice flour, served with coconut milk and melted brown sugar

list.shortDescription: A traditional Indonesian dry cookie made from crumbly sweet white mung bean powder, commonly found in Java and served during Lebaran, Christmas, and Imlek.

cover.altText: Kue satu: Kue satu

list.shortDescription: A Southeast Asian steamed snack made from rice flour, coconut milk, and other ingredients in a mold pan called a talam, meaning “tray,” or in individual cups.

cover.altText: Kue talam: Kue Talam

list.shortDescription: A cold, often spicy noodle dish with beef from the Koryo-saram cuisine of ethnic Koreans in the former Soviet Union, a variation on janchi-guksu.

cover.altText: Kuksu: Kuksi, the Russo-Korean version of janchi-guksu (banquet noodles)

list.shortDescription: A Nigerian peanut snack first made by the Nupe people, eaten alone or with garri soakings, Hausa koko, fura, and akamu, and sometimes ground for salad, suya, or kilishi.

cover.altText: Kuli-kuli: This is an image of food from

list.shortDescription: A traditional Central Javanese salad eaten alone for vegetarian meals or as a side dish. An inscription from the Medang Mataram era, around the 9th century CE, mentions it.
A Filipino deep-fried doughnut from the Maguindanao people, made with rice flour, duck eggs, and sugar, traditionally fried in spirals with a creamy flavor similar to pancakes.
A dome-shaped savoury pirog from southern Russia’s Cossack communities, filled with chicken or turkey, eggs, onions, and kasha or rice. It is served on special occasions in most of Russia.

cover.altText: Kurnik: Kurnik, tradional big russian pie for celebration table. Filled with slices of chicken, mushrooms, blini, rice, eggs

list.shortDescription: An Armenian dish of roasted bull’s head, once associated with lower-income groups but now widely consumed and especially popular in Gyumri.

A Japanese bento style that arranges food as animals, plants, traditions, or media characters, often pandas, bears, Pikachu, or Totoro. It developed as a playful children’s meal in the 1990s and became especially popular among mothers.

cover.altText: Kyaraben: A Kyaraben depicting pandas

list.shortDescription: Spätzle from Swabia, Baden, and Allgäu is layered with grated Emmentaler or Bergkäse, baked until the cheese melts, and topped with fried onions; it is also served in Vorarlberg, Tyrol, Liechtenstein, and Switzerland.

cover.altText: Käsespätzle, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Turkish börek from Sivas, Elazığ, Malatya, Kahramanmaraş, and Osmaniye provinces, popular among Turkish people.

cover.altText: Kömbe: "Kömbe"s from Osmaniye, Turkey

list.shortDescription: A Chadian breakfast porridge made from milk and wheat berries or rice, thickened with flour or millet paste and sweetened with peanut butter or brown sugar, then served hot with fruit, ginger, or peanuts.

cover.altText: La bouillie: This is an image with the theme " Home + Habitat in Africa " from:

list.shortDescription: A Spanish dried ham made from a pig’s shoulder. Lacón galego comes from Galicia, where pigs may be raised on natural feeds such as acorns, cereals, and chestnuts before slaughter.

cover.altText: Lacón Gallego: Lacón

list.shortDescription: A Seychellois dish of plantains or sweet potatoes, prepared with salted fish as a savory dish or with coconut milk, sugar, nutmeg, and vanilla as a dessert.
A pickled bonito dish eaten as a mezze in the Balkans and Middle East. Lakerda made from one-year-old bonito migrating through the Bosphorus is especially prized.

cover.altText: Lakerda: Lakerda steaks (center) at a shop located at Kapani market, Thessaloniki

list.shortDescription: A Sri Lankan dish introduced by the country’s Dutch Burgher population. Its name derives from the Dutch lomprijst, meaning a packet or lump of rice, and it is believed to have roots in the Indonesian lemper.

cover.altText: Lamprais: A traditional Sri Lanka burgher dish, Lamprais, cooked in a banana leaf

list.shortDescription: A Florentine sandwich of cattle’s fourth and final stomach, the abomasum, slow-cooked in vegetable broth with herbs, chopped, and served in a bread roll with spicy or green sauce.

cover.altText: Lampredotto: Lampredotto (Bovine abomasum), pre-boiled on the market. Foto made in Florence, Italy

list.shortDescription: A German dish of ground beef liver or pork mixed with bread, eggs, parsley, and spices, shaped into dumplings and boiled in beef broth or fried in lard.

cover.altText: Leberknödel: Leberknoedelsuppe

list.shortDescription: A Filipino spit-roasted chicken marinated in garlic, onion, black pepper, soy sauce, and patis, stuffed with lemongrass and roasted over charcoal. Served with rice or puso, atchara pickles, and a calamansi-chili dip.

cover.altText: Lechon manok: Conching's Native Lechon Manok

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian crêpe made with wheat flour, eggs, milk, and sugar, folded in half and served with fillings or toppings such as bananas, condensed milk, cheese, or chocolate sprinkles.

cover.altText: Leker Cake: Kue Lekker, pancake, Semarang, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: A French dish of lobster meat in a rich wine sauce, stuffed into the shell and browned. The sauce often includes egg yolks and brandy, with an oven-browned Gruyère crust; powdered mustard was originally included.

cover.altText: Lobster Thermidor: Lobster Thermidor (at the left of the plate)

list.shortDescription: A rice dish in contemporary Hawaiian cuisine, pairing white rice with a hamburger patty, brown gravy, and a sunny-side-up egg. Modern versions may include grilled onions, pickled vegetables, macaroni, or potato salad.

cover.altText: Loco moco: Loco moco

list.shortDescription: A Finnish salmon chowder of fillets, boiled potatoes, carrots, and leeks, made creamy with cream or whole milk and seasoned with dill, allspice, salt, and black pepper.

cover.altText: Lohikeitto: Finnish traditional salmon soup (lohikeitto), Helsinki

list.shortDescription: A liquorice candy sold in Finland and Sweden by Chymos and later Fazer, with a soft liquorice-flavoured core in a hard, sugary aniseed coating.

cover.altText: London drops, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Javanese vegetable salad dressed with peanut sauce. Its sauce shares ingredients with pecel but is typically much sweeter, reflecting classic Matraman cuisine.

cover.altText: Lotek: Lotek, the traditional food of Yogyakarta, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: An Armenian and Azerbaijani kebab of minced mutton, or sheep and beef blended in equal parts, cooked on skewers with onion, sheep-tail fat, salt, pepper, and optional sumac.

cover.altText: Lula kebab: Lyulya kebab served in lavash, and with fried tomatoes, pomegranate grains, onion and lemon pieces

list.shortDescription: A hamburger or cheeseburger built around one or more glazed doughnuts instead of a bun. Its origin is disputed, and it generally runs from about 800 to 1,500 calories.

cover.altText: Luther Burger, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Ugandan stew or sauce made with smoked young leaves of the Ndiizi banana plant. Reserved for Buganda’s kings and princes from 1887, it is now eaten by the Baganda generally and other Ugandan ethnic groups.

cover.altText: Luwombo: This is an image of food from

list.shortDescription: A traditional Beijing street-food dish of pork, pork lung, intestines, liver, and tofu, served with bing bread and sometimes fermented bean curd or chives sauce.

cover.altText: Luzhu Huoshao: Moved from Tianqiao to Maliandao

list.shortDescription: A Fujianese dish of deep-fried pork and sliced water chestnuts in sweet-and-sour sauce, colored red with red yeast rice; the sauce may include ketchup, soy sauce, and rice vinegar.

cover.altText: Lychee pork, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A traditional Finnish stew of pork belly fried in butter with onions and flour, then simmered in seasoned water and served with mashed potato, pickled cucumber, and lingonberry.

cover.altText: Läskisoosi: Finnish "läskisoosi" or "sianlihakastike", fatty pork belly stewed in brown gravy, served with boiled potatoes, pickles and red beet

list.shortDescription: A Central African fish dish seasoned with roasted spices and wrapped in cassava or banana leaves, eaten in the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sometimes with fried plantains and rice.

cover.altText: Maboké: Cuisine Centrafricaine

list.shortDescription: Mache, also called matse, is a Laguna, Philippines, dish of glutinous rice balls. Plain or pandan-flavored galapong surrounds toasted sesame seeds and sugar, with a coating of glutinous rice flour or powdered sugar.
A Javanese snack from Ponorogo, East Java, made by fermenting black sticky rice into tapai and cooking it into sweet dodol.

cover.altText: Madumongso: Madumongso

list.shortDescription: A Libyan Jewish dish of hollowed root vegetables packed with ground meat and spices, fried, and simmered in tomato sauce. Potatoes are usual; eggplant, zucchini, onions, and bell peppers may also be used.

cover.altText: Mafrum: מפרום וקוסקוס ביתי מסורתי

list.shortDescription: A Southeast Asian confection of glutinous-rice dough around palm sugar, rolled in grated coconut and colored with pandan or suji extract, then boiled until the filling melts.

cover.altText: Onde-onde, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: Putri salju is an Indonesian dry cake shaped like crescents and covered in powdered sugar. Its name means “snow princess,” referring to the coating’s resemblance to snow.

cover.altText: Putri salju cake: Kue putri salju, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: Low-density, dry, egg-based sweet sponge biscuits shaped like large fingers, called savoiardi or boudoirs, and used in trifles, charlottes, gateau linings, and tiramisu.

cover.altText: Savoiarde PAT: Lady Fingers

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian snack made from diced soft inner cattle skin, sun-dried until hard, then fried in hot oil until expanded and crisp. Vacuum-sealed to prolong its crispiness.

cover.altText: Skin Crackers: Kerupuk kulit (kerupuk jangek) sudah digoreng sekali

list.shortDescription: A Finnish vegetable soup cooked in milk with butter, potatoes, carrots, peas, cauliflower, and other seasonal vegetables.

cover.altText: Summer soup, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Igbo Nigerian dish of yam cooked with spinach or ugu, red pepper, onions, crayfish, oil bean, seasoning cubes, and salt. It is especially eaten during the annual New Yam Festival.

cover.altText: Yam porridge, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Chinese fried sesame egg cake of flour, peanut oil, egg, sugar, malt sugar, and baking soda. Sesame-coated dough pieces are fried until they crack open like a smiling mouth, making them a popular Lunar New Year dish.

cover.altText: Zhimazao: A plate of yau gokes and sesame cookie balls was provided by club house in Hong Kong

list.shortDescription: A soft, sweet Indonesian cake tied to South Kalimantan’s Banjar kue and also found in Malay cuisine. It belongs to a 41-cake tradition for occasions such as weddings and is common during Ramadan for iftar.
The large fruit of Pangium edule, a tall tree native to Southeast Asia’s mangrove swamps, is poisonous but becomes edible when fermented.

cover.altText: buah keluak, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Finnish oven-baked casserole of cabbage, ground meat, rice or pearl barley, onion, marjoram, and a little syrup or molasses, usually served with lingonberry or crowberry jam.

cover.altText: cabbage casserole: Very tasty indeed!

list.shortDescription: A Chinese noodle associated with Shanxi, made by thinly slicing a block of dough into boiling water. The cooked ribbons are fairly thick and chewy; Datong’s variation is the most famous.

cover.altText: dāoxiāo miàn: A Chinese traditional food named sliced noodles

list.shortDescription: A Korean variety of bibimbap with several kinds of namul over white rice, served with soy sauce (ganjang), grilled fish, and some jeon.

cover.altText: heotjesabap: Heotjesabab at a restaurant in Andong, South Korea 대한민국 안동시의 한 음식점에서 헛제사밥

list.shortDescription: Herring soup is a thick fish soup made by combining red herring with water and barley meal into a thick mixture.

A Korean bibimbap of steamed rice mixed with sliced or cubed raw fish, lettuce, cucumber, sesame leaves, sesame oil, and chogochujang. It may use halibut, sea bass, rockfish, tuna, salmon, or whitefish.

cover.altText: hoe-deopbap, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Japanese dessert from Shibuya that emerged during the Japanese asset price bubble and is often served at karaoke bars. Also called Shibuya toast, brick toast, or hanitō.

cover.altText: honey toast: 巧克力嘉年華蜜糖土司

list.shortDescription: A Spanish meat pie of Salamanca and Ávila, made with flour and yeast and filled with pork loin, spicy chorizo, and hard-boiled eggs.

cover.altText: hornazo: Hornazo

list.shortDescription: A South Korean filled pancake and popular street food, brought from Qing dynasty China to Joseon Korea in the 19th century.

cover.altText: hotteok, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Mexican breakfast of eggs, garlic, tomatoes, and chile de árbol, usually served with refried beans and corn tortillas. In Mexico City, it comes with salsa verde; in Oaxaca, it becomes an omelet under spicy sauce with epazote.
A Mexican breakfast of sunny-side-up eggs fried in lard with red or green chile sauce, served with grated aged cheese in the ranchero tradition of rural Mexican farms.

cover.altText: huevos rancheros: whats4dinnersolutions.wordpress.com/2011/08/04/huevos-ran

list.shortDescription: A baked bun from Fuzhou, Fujian province, China, with a leavened flour-and-water shell and a meat filling marinated with sugar, soy sauce, pepper, and scallion. Popular in Taiwan’s night markets and mini food stalls.
A small Korean pan-fried rice cake made with glutinous rice flour, honey, and seasonal edible flower petals, including rhododendron. It is eaten during Samjinnal and Buddha’s Birthday.

cover.altText: hwajeon: Cooking for Hwajeon(Flower Rice Cake)

list.shortDescription: An Ottoman eggplant and meat dish, with lamb or beef cubes atop eggplant grilled until the skin burns, then puréed, seasoned, and thickened with béchamel sauce.

cover.altText: hünkârbeğendi: Hünkarbeğendi, un plat de carn i albergina a la cuina turca

list.shortDescription: A brittle pastry cone, usually made from a waffle-textured wafer, allows ice cream to be carried and eaten without a bowl or spoon. Styles include Cornetto, sugar-coated, and chocolate-coated cones.

cover.altText: ice cream cone: Strawberry Ice Cream Cone

list.shortDescription: A Kumamoto confection of sweet potato wrapped in wheat flour, dango rice flour, and salt, then steamed; azuki bean paste became the mainstream filling from the Showa era.

cover.altText: ikinaridango: Ikinari-dango , traditional confectionery of Kumamoto prefecture

list.shortDescription: A Japanese preparation of sashimi using live seafood, most often fish but also octopus, shrimp, or lobster. The animal may seem alive when served, a practice criticized for concerns about its suffering.

cover.altText: ikizukuri, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A North Korean dish made with rice, kimchi, soybean paste and soybean oil. Steamed rice is wrapped in a light skin of leftover soybean paste and dressed with chili sauce, creating a meat-like texture.
A South Sulawesi fried dumpling filled with rice vermicelli, vegetables, potatoes, and eggs, dipped in a spicy, sweet-and-sour sauce before eating. Popular in Makassarese cuisine.

cover.altText: jalangkote, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A savory Louisiana rice dish shaped by African, Spanish, and French influences, with meat or seafood, vegetables, rice, spices, and tomato. The blending of regional styles has produced cultural and regional variations.

cover.altText: jambalaya: A savory rice dish of mixed origins that developed in the U.S. state of Louisiana

list.shortDescription: A traditional Chinese snack made from rice or glutinous rice, also known as bipang or berondong beras. Chinese immigrants introduced and sold it in Indonesia as a snack.

cover.altText: jipang: Jipang beras, a kind of snack made of rice from Indonesia. Product of Berlian, Surabaya

list.shortDescription: A Finnish Christmas pastry made from puff pastry in a star or pinwheel shape, filled with prune jam and dusted with icing sugar. Other shapes and jams are also possible.

cover.altText: joulutorttu: Finnish Christmas pastries filled with prune marmalade and topped with powdered sugar

list.shortDescription: A Mayan soup from Guatemala made with chompipe turkey. Its name comes from the Q'eqchi' words kak, meaning red, and ik; in 2007 it was declared part of Guatemala’s Intangible Cultural Heritage.

cover.altText: kak'ik: Kac-iq, a traditional food of Alta Verpaz, Guatemala, being served in Antigua Guatemala at Fonda de la Calle Real

list.shortDescription: Japanese shaved ice flavored with syrup and sweetened, often with condensed milk. In the Heian period, winter ice was shaved and served with sweet syrup to the aristocracy.

cover.altText: kakigōri, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Finnish fish dish from Savonia, with fish baked inside a loaf of bread. It is especially popular in Kuopio, which hosts an annual kalakukko baking contest.

cover.altText: kalakukko: Traditional Savonian (Eastern Finland) 'Kalakukko' made with European Perch and pork belly

list.shortDescription: A Dutch fast-food dish of fries in a metal tray, topped with döner meat and melted Gouda, then layered with iceberg lettuce, garlic sauce and sambal. Created in Rotterdam in 2003, its name means “hairdressing salon.”

cover.altText: kapsalon: Kapsalon food

list.shortDescription: A Sundanese raw vegetable salad from West Java, Indonesia, traditionally made with long beans, cucumbers, sprouts, cabbage, lemon basil, chayote, and eggplant in peanut sauce, usually served with hot rice, tofu, tempeh, and krupuk.

cover.altText: karedok: Karedok (Sundanese salad in peanut sauce) served in a nice restaurant in Ubud, Bali, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: A Turkish dish of eggplant stuffed with a sautéed mixture of chopped onion, garlic, black pepper, tomato, optional green pepper, parsley, and ground meat. The eggplant may be fried or roasted and is often served with rice.

cover.altText: karnıyarık: A typical summertime meal in Turkey: "Karnıyarık", Turkish pilav with rice and 2 types of "şehriye" ("orzo" and pasta "capelli d'angelo"), "cacık" and a small salad for one

list.shortDescription: A Turkish kebab peculiar to Hatay and Antakya, made with tomatoes, peppers, minced meat, and spices, then baked in paper to retain its juices and flavors.

cover.altText: kağıt kebabı: "Kağıt kebabı" is a veal and vegetables dish from the Turkish cuisine, made in the oven

list.shortDescription: A Betawi spicy omelet of glutinous rice and egg, served with serundeng, fried shallots, and dried shrimp. Eaten as a snack, it has become popular at the annual Jakarta Fair.

cover.altText: kerak telor: kerak telor very unique, because it is made of rice and chicken or duck eggs, which are put together and cooked on a small cauldron and firewood

list.shortDescription: An Acehnese dish of dried skipjack or tuna, cleaned, boiled, dried, and stored dry and moisture-free; the firm fish, also called wood fish, can keep for years.

cover.altText: keumamah: Keumamah adalah makanan tradisional Aceh yang dibuat dari ikan tongkol yang direbus dan dijemur di bawah sinar matahari

list.shortDescription: A Thai dish influenced by Teochew cuisine: stewed pork knuckles in condensed pottage are sliced over steamed rice and served with half-spiced corned eggs and pickled mustard greens.

cover.altText: khao kha mu: Khao kha mu thailand

list.shortDescription: A South Asian dish of rice and lentils (dal), with variations including bajra and mung dal khichri. In several regions of India, especially the north, it is among the first solid foods babies eat.

cover.altText: khichri: Dal Khichdi

list.shortDescription: A Syrian dish of lamb or beef chunks and kibbeh in safarjaliyeh, a broth of quince, pomegranate juice, pomegranate molasses, and beef broth. It is a variation of Levantine kibbeh.

cover.altText: kibbeh safarjaliyeh: A bowl of kibbeh safarjaliyeh made with beef

list.shortDescription: A Hausaland jerky made from beef, lamb, mutton, or chevon, seasoned with salt, pepper and spices, then smoked, dried and sun-dried for preservation. In Niger, it is commonly eaten with pap or cassava flakes (garri).

cover.altText: kilishi: Kilishi is made from sliced and dried beef, coated with peanut paste "Labu" in Hausa

list.shortDescription: A Dutch-influenced Indonesian coconut cake from Manado, North Sulawesi, made with flour, sugar, milk, butter, coconut flesh, and coconut juice.

cover.altText: klappertaart: Klappertaart! Coconut custard and meringue

list.shortDescription: A Ukrainian dish in which a filling is enclosed in dough, then baked or sometimes deep-fried; knishes are also characteristic of Ashkenazi Jewish cuisine.

cover.altText: knish: Knishes (knyshes) stuffed with mashed potatoes and fried onions

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian sweet dessert of palm or coconut sugar, coconut milk, and pandanus leaf, with bananas or other additions such as pumpkin, sweet potato, jackfruit, plantains, cassava, rice balls, tapioca pearls, and kolang-kaling.

cover.altText: kolak: Kolak pisang dan ubi, Jakarta, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: Egypt’s national dish and a popular street food, koshari combines pasta, Egyptian fried rice, vermicelli, and brown lentils, with chickpeas, garlicky tomato sauce, garlic vinegar, and crispy fried onions on top.

cover.altText: koshari: This is an image of food from

list.shortDescription: A Polish pork cutlet covered in breadcrumbs, comparable to schnitzel, cotoletta, côtelette de veau frite, milanesa, cachopo, and tonkatsu.

cover.altText: kotlet schabowy: Kotlet schabowy — fried breaded pork made of tenderloin. As served at a restaurant in Poznan, Poland

list.shortDescription: Polish semi-soft milk toffee candies whose handmade form has a hard, crisp exterior and a fluid interior.

cover.altText: krówki, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian street-food pancake with a soft, fluffy center and thin, crispy edges, popular in Jakarta and other major cities. Also known as serabi Jakarta or kue cucur tipis.

cover.altText: kue ape: Traditional Indonesian Snack

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian coconut waffle made with coconut and starch-based batter, cooked in a special molded pan and served as a traditional Betawi snack of Jakarta.

cover.altText: kue rangi, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Turkish baked potato with a range of fillings, a popular fast food across the Balkans. Its name reached Anatolia through Balkan Turks and derives from a Palatine or Alemannic word for potato.

cover.altText: kumpir, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Turkish stew of white beans in olive oil with onion and tomato paste or sauce, sometimes other vegetables or pastirma. Often served with cacık and rice or bulgur, and considered Turkey’s national dish.

cover.altText: kuru fasulye: Kuru Fasulye

list.shortDescription: Small, slightly sweet Lithuanian cakes made from leavened dough and poppy seeds, served on Christmas Eve dry, soaked in poppy milk, or with cranberry kissel.

cover.altText: kūčiukai: Kūčiukai

list.shortDescription: A Chinese handmade noodle of soft wheat flour, common in northern China. The dough is twisted, stretched, and folded into strands, with length and thickness determined by the number of folds.

cover.altText: lamian: ​兰州安泊尔牛肉面。

list.shortDescription: A Batak snack from Tapanuli, North Sumatra, Indonesia, made from itak, a rice traditionally ground using minimal equipment.

An Italian pasta dish of wide, flat sheets layered with meat, dairy, vegetables, and sauces, topped with grated cheese and baked. Regional variations exist across Italy, with Americanized versions found worldwide.

cover.altText: lasagna: Lasagne served on a white plate

list.shortDescription: A yogurt-based drink with a smoothie-like consistency. “Lassi” is a Hindi loanword, recorded by 1882, though its ultimate origin remains uncertain.

cover.altText: lassi: A summer drink prepared in India

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian dish of mixed vegetables, coconut, and minced meat or blood, seasoned with herbs and spices and commonly found in restaurants and warungs in Bali.

cover.altText: lawar: Lawar (mixed vegetables) and Babi Guling (roasted suckling pig), cuisine of Bali

list.shortDescription: A Lebanese dessert of semolina pudding scented with orange blossom water and rose water, layered with qishta and topped with ground pistachios, honey, or qatir.

cover.altText: layali lubnan: לילות בירות קינוח של פודינג סולת

list.shortDescription: Polish pasta of wheat, rye, or buckwheat dough rolled thin, cut into triangles or rectangles, and boiled. In Poland, it is mixed with fried or soured cabbage and small pieces of sausage, meat, and mushrooms.

cover.altText: lazanki, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Dutch dish of batter-coated white fish—originally whiting, now also cod, pangasius, or pollock—deep-fried and often served with tartar sauce. Its beginnings are uncertain, though IJmuiden is a possible birthplace.

cover.altText: lekkerbekje: A traditional Dutch fish dish called lekkerbekje : originally a filet of cod fish in batter, deep fried, served with French fries, sauce and salad. It can also be served as a snack with sauce only

list.shortDescription: A Malay and Minangkabau rice dish of glutinous rice, coconut milk, and salt, cooked in banana-lined bamboo tubes to prevent the rice from sticking.

cover.altText: lemang, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian savoury snack of glutinous rice filled with seasoned shredded chicken, fish, abon, or serundeng. The filling is rolled inside the rice, then wrapped in banana leaf, corn husk, oil paper, plastic, or foil.

cover.altText: lemper: Lemper

list.shortDescription: Croatian licitars are colorfully decorated biscuits made from sweet honey dough and symbolizing Zagreb. They belong to Croatia and Slovenia’s cultural heritage and are given as ornamental gifts at weddings and Valentine’s Day.

cover.altText: licitar: Another picture of Croatian licitars available in Croatia

list.shortDescription: A Chinese noodle dish of thin, elastic flour-and-egg noodles. Cantonese-style lo mein is topped or accompanied by char siu, beef brisket, wontons, or vegetables, and may be served with broth.

Leavened dough balls are deep-fried, then soaked in syrup or honey, and sometimes coated with cinnamon or other ingredients. Al-Baghdadi described the dessert in the 13th century as luqmat al-qādi, “judge’s morsels.”

cover.altText: lokma: Lokma

list.shortDescription: Lokša, a flatbread-like potato pancake popular in Slovakia and South Moravia, where lokše also refers to wide noodles added to soups.

cover.altText: lokša, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian rice cake made by rolling rice inside a banana leaf, boiling it, and cutting the cylinder into small cakes. It serves as a staple replacement for steamed rice and is also found in Malaysia and Singapore.

cover.altText: lontong: Lontong; Indonesian compressed rice

list.shortDescription: A rice-cake dish from Pemalang Regency, Central Java, serving sliced cakes in a yellow, watery broth colored by turmeric and spices, with fried shallots, serundeng, and krupuk as garnishes.

cover.altText: lontong dekem: Lontong sayur, rice cakes served with coconut milk curry

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian finger food from Semarang, Central Java, filled with rebung, egg, dried shrimp, and chicken meat or prawn in a crepe-like lumpia wrapper.

cover.altText: lumpia Semarang: Lumpia (juga ditulis: Lunpia / Loenpia) Gang Lombok Semarang

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian sweet cake of glutinous rice, banana leaves, coconut, and brown sugar sauce, shaped cylindrically or in triangles and served with thick palm sugar syrup and shredded coconut.

cover.altText: lupis: Sticky rice served with brown sugar

list.shortDescription: A Hungarian flatbread made historically from the last bits of bread dough and baked at the front of a brick or clay oven, served hot during the bread-baking day’s breakfast.

cover.altText: lángos: Langos Eger Hungary

list.shortDescription: Macaroni and cheese pairs macaroni with cheese sauce, usually cheddar. It traces back to medieval English cheese-and-pasta casseroles; the traditional dish is baked in a casserole, though it may also be made in a saucepan.

cover.altText: macaroni and cheese: Mac n Cheese from BRC Gastropub

list.shortDescription: An Italian soup of macaroni with Parmesan cheese, one of the most common dishes in Italian inns in the early 19th century.

cover.altText: macaroni soup: Soup Macaroni in Hong Kong with egg, toast and tea as breakfast

list.shortDescription: A soft, brightly colored Turkish toffee sold as street food, prepared with numerous herbs and spices and rooted in the Ottoman herbal paste mesir macunu.

cover.altText: macun şekeri: Macun, a Turkish sweet food, especially for kids during popular celebrations ("bayram")

list.shortDescription: A northern European baked-pasta staple, this casserole combines cooked macaroni with eggs and milk, plus meat, vegetables, or fish, and is topped with cheese or breadcrumbs.

cover.altText: makaroni schotel: Quite typical pot of Finnish macaroni casserole made with textured soy and topped with cheese

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian traditional snack made from wheat flour-based batter and cooked in a special mold pan, commonly sold in traditional markets.

cover.altText: pukis: Kue pancong di pasar Rantepao

list.shortDescription: A sweet Finnish potato casserole from Päijät-Häme. Puréed potatoes are mixed with wheat flour and rested to develop sweetness, then combined with milk and baked until thickened and caramelized.

cover.altText: sweetened potato casserole: Jouluruokaa. Äiti teki

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian Chinese wafer snack made by clasping egg batter in a heated iron mold over a charcoal stove, commonly found in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Brunei.

cover.altText: uih sepit: Kue semprong, crispy rolls made of rice flour and coconut milk

list.shortDescription: Sicilian stuffed cookies from Modica, shaped like half-moons and filled with almonds, walnuts, chocolate, sugar, cinnamon, cloves, and minced beef.

cover.altText: 'Mpanatigghi: Tapas de empanadillas rellenas de atún y salsa de tomate con huevo cocido

list.shortDescription: Traditional cookies from Messina and Catania in Italy, shaped into slightly flattened golden spheres and made with flour, sugar, almonds, cinnamon, egg whites, and vanilla.

cover.altText: 'Nzuddi: Gli 'Nzuddi messinesi della Madonna della Lettera

list.shortDescription: A traditional Portuguese wheat bread from the Alentejo region, traditionally made in homes with the dough baked in communal ovens or by small bakeries.

cover.altText: Alentejano bread: Encontramos “pan portugués” (pão de testa) en Isla Cristina, porque esta zona de Huelva (España) tiene mucha influencia portuguesa. Un pan riquísimo 🥖❤️

list.shortDescription: A festive Burmese rice dish served at wedding receptions and almsgiving feasts, typically paired with traditional chicken or mutton curry.

An Indonesian-Aceh noodle dish from Pidie and Pidie Jaya, topped with a thick sauce of tomato, chili, coconut milk, ground peanuts, shallot, garlic, lemongrass, and citrus leaf, plus vegetables, cucumber, and krupuk.

cover.altText: Caluk noodles: Mie paling ekonomis dengan kualitas terbaik di Aceh

list.shortDescription: A boiled potato dish from the Canary Islands, served with mojo rojo, a chili pepper garlic sauce. Often paired with meat or fish, but also eaten alone as tapas and dipped into shared sauces without cutlery.

cover.altText: Canarian wrinkly potatoes: Papas arrugadas con mojo

list.shortDescription: A Czech-style hot dog pairs a cooked sausage with a partially sliced bun, with the sausage traditionally grilled or steamed.

cover.altText: Czech-style hot dog: Jersey breakfast dog, taken by me

list.shortDescription: A sweet, coiled pastry made by winding thin sheets of phyllo dough into a spiral with ground almonds, almond paste, or walnuts, then frying or baking it.

cover.altText: M'hancha: Mhancha

list.shortDescription: An Indian offal dish of cow, goat, or sheep brain served in gravy, also known as Maghaz or Bheja in Pakistani and Bangladeshi cuisine.

cover.altText: Magaj: This is a plate of Magaj Masala (Goat's brain masala) i had at a Pakistani restaurant in Salmabad, Bahrain

list.shortDescription: Finnish street food pairing French fries with sliced sausage, deep-fried in fat or baked in the oven and served with condiments; it is also popular elsewhere.

cover.altText: Makkaraperunat: Makkaraperunat-portion, cubed sausage, french fries and excessively ketchup and mustard

list.shortDescription: A fried-cheese ball found in western Switzerland, especially in villages along Lake Leman. Swiss mercenaries devised it during the siege of Sevastopol, and its name comes from the Battle of Malakoff.

cover.altText: Malakoff: Deux Malakoffs vaudois

list.shortDescription: A Sri Lankan condiment of lightly sautéed, shredded greens with fresh coconut, spices, and chili, served at almost every meal.

cover.altText: Mallung: Mallung is lightly sautéed greens, cooked with coconut, spicies and chilli

list.shortDescription: A British confectionery with a spherical malted milk centre coated in milk chocolate, launched by Mars Inc. in 1937. Its slogan is “The lighter way to enjoy chocolate.”

cover.altText: Maltesers: A pile of Maltesers candies and one split in half

list.shortDescription: A traditional potato dish of the Grisons in Switzerland. Boiled potatoes are peeled, grated, mixed with flour, and slowly fried in butter with constant stirring until golden balls or crumbs form.

cover.altText: Maluns, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A traditional Thai sweet of mango slowly cooked with sugar and salt, optionally coconut milk, then dried into soft, chewy golden fruit leather shaped as circles, flowers, or spirals.

cover.altText: Mamuang kuan: มะม่วงกวน

list.shortDescription: A popular, hot, spicy, easily prepared Indo-Chinese soup from Meghalaya, India, available at many restaurants and street food carts. Despite its name, it does not resemble food normally found in Manchuria.

cover.altText: Manchow soup: A bowl of chicken Manchow soup with crispy-fried noodles

list.shortDescription: A Ukrainian pastry filled with cottage cheese or quark. Its name comes from the Polish term małdrzyk, originally a measure of grain.

cover.altText: Mandrykas: Сирна начинка мандрики

list.shortDescription: An Indian chicken dish native to Mangalore and Udupi in Karnataka, called kori sukka or kori ajadina in Tulu. It may be prepared dry or as a semi-gravy; “sukka” derives from Hindi “sukha,” meaning “dry.”

cover.altText: Mangalorean Chicken Sukka: A Mangalorean dish consisting of chicken in a thick coconut and red-chilli based gravy

list.shortDescription: Spongy sweet breads from northwestern Spain, traditionally produced in Astorga, in the province of León, and the nearby Maragateria comarca. Their flavor resembles pound cake.

cover.altText: Mantecadas de Astorga: Mantecada, a type of Spanish muffin

list.shortDescription: A Batak chicken dish from Indonesia, usually served at certain customary feasts. The chicken is baked, then cooked with chicken blood, andaliman, and garlic powder.
A Chongqing dish of blood curds and tripe with mung bean sprouts, fully cooked in a communal bowl of mala-seasoned oily broth.

cover.altText: Mao xue wang, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A northeastern Nigerian soup of the Margi, made with Lake Chad fish, sorrel, spinach, tomatoes, and bean sprouts in tamarind-flavored broth, garnished with scented garlic. Served alone or with pounded yam, tuwo, or rice.

cover.altText: Margi special: This is an image of food from

list.shortDescription: A Bolivian bread roll made with wheat flour, salt, water, and yeast, with a crusty exterior and commonly found in Bolivian bakeries.

cover.altText: Marraqueta, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An American soup combining lump Maryland crab meat, tomatoes, corn, potato, celery or celery leaves, peas, onion, and Old Bay, with water, shellfish stock, or fish stock as the liquid.

cover.altText: Maryland crab soup: four large pots of Maryland Crab Soup

list.shortDescription: Cebu’s glutinous rice balls enclose chopped roasted peanuts and muscovado. Made with sweetened galapong, they are boiled until they float or steamed, then traditionally wrapped in banana leaves for sale.

cover.altText: Masi: Masi (glutinous rice balls) with peanut butter filling (Philippines)

list.shortDescription: Maldivian maskurolhi is a coconut-and-tuna chutney. In the Maldives, it is eaten with baipen during Ramadan.
A Ugandan meal of green East African Highland bananas, carefully peeled, cooked, and mashed or pounded. Steamed in Uganda and Rwanda, it is considered a national dish in both countries.

cover.altText: Matoke: This is an image of "African people at work" from

list.shortDescription: Mattar paneer, also called matar or mutter paneer, is a modern North Indian vegetarian restaurant dish pairing peas and paneer in a tomato-based sauce seasoned with garam masala.

cover.altText: Mattar paneer: Café Ilang-Ilang Manila Hotel heritage dishes since 1920s

list.shortDescription: Mazamorra, also called masamorra, is a name shared by numerous traditional dishes across the regional cuisines of Spain and Hispanic America.

cover.altText: Mazamorra, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: Abruzzo rolls of lamb offal wrapped in endive leaves and tied with lamb casings. A traditional PAT product recognized by Italy’s agriculture ministry, they are widespread in the mountains, especially around Teramo.
An Indonesian noodle soup of bakso meatballs with yellow noodles or rice vermicelli, familiar in Chinese Indonesian, Javanese, and Malay cuisine and distinguished from soto mie by its meatballs.

cover.altText: Meatball noodles: A bowl of Indonesian bakso, with noodle and bean sprouts

list.shortDescription: A Ukrainian honey cake and a foundational dessert of Lviv regional cuisine, made with spices, nuts, and raisins, with buckwheat honey preferred. The name can also denote a hard honey cookie.

cover.altText: Medivnyk, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Hokkaidō delicacy of chum salmon kidney, originally Ainu, salt-pickled until dark brownish black. It has a sweet umami taste and is served with alcohol or as a side dish.

cover.altText: Mefun: An Ainu "set meal" with venison and mountain vegetable soup ( yuk ohaw ), fermented salmon liver ( mefun ) and rice mixed with grains. Served at Cafe Poronno, Akan Kotan, Hokkaido, Japan

list.shortDescription: A Lebanese dessert of floured rice pudding spiced with anise, caraway, and cinnamon, topped with coconut and nuts. Served for child births and at Christmas to celebrate Jesus’s birth.

cover.altText: Meghli: Meghli

list.shortDescription: A Filipino pork and liver stew cooked in tomato sauce with carrots and potatoes. Also called ginamay or ginagmay, it contains no tripe, hominy, or red chili sauce.

cover.altText: Menudo: Menudo served at Oriental Valley Filipino Cuisine in the Rancho Peñasquitos neighborhood of San Diego

list.shortDescription: A traditional Mexican soup of cow’s stomach tripe in broth with a red chili pepper base, also known as Mondongo, pancita, or mole de panza.

cover.altText: Menudo: Menudo, or pancita is a traditional Mexican soup, made with beef stomach (tripe) in broth with a red chili pepper base

list.shortDescription: A Dutch confection with a marzipan layer around a sweet filling and chocolate-covered ends. The small version contains cream; the larger reuzemergpijp adds sponge cake and may include berry jam.

cover.altText: Mergpijpje, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A French salad of assorted small young greens from Provence, traditionally including chervil, arugula, leafy lettuces, and endive.

cover.altText: Mesclun: Mesclun, petits légumes marinés et chèvre chaud aux herbes sur toasts

list.shortDescription: A German preparation of minced raw pork seasoned with salt and black pepper, often spread on half a bread roll with raw onion. Since the 1950s, it has also been shaped into a hedgehog for buffets.

cover.altText: Mett: Mettbrötchen

list.shortDescription: An Acehnese dodol-like cake made with flour, sugar, butter, and pineapple and lemon juice, giving it a yellow hue. Served at weddings, Eid al-Fitr, and Eid al-Adha.

cover.altText: Meuseukat: Meuseukat, a kind of Acehnese cakes

list.shortDescription: A spicy noodle soup of the Toba Batak in North Sumatra, served in broth made with coconut milk and andaliman, with thick mie lidi noodles resembling spaghetti. It is also a specialty of Sibolga and Tapanuli.

cover.altText: Mi Gomak, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian beef noodle soup from Bandung, West Java, made with noodles in rich beef consommé, kikil, bean sprouts, bakso, kaffir lime juice, celery, scallion, and fried shallot; some recipes include beef tripe.

cover.altText: Mi Kocok: Mie kocok

list.shortDescription: A Wuhan deep-fried, donut-shaped snack made with soy milk, rice milk, flour, sesame, and chopped Chinese scallion. It is usually salty, with a sweeter sweet-potato variant.

cover.altText: Mianwo: Mianwo of Wuhan

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian variation on mie goreng from Lhokseumawe, made with instant noodles stir-fried in a herb-and-spice sauce and served slightly soupy, sometimes with egg, fried onions, or mustard greens.

cover.altText: Mie Bangladesh: Bangladesh noodle from Medan, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian noodle soup specialty of Palembang, South Sumatra: large yellow wheat noodles in coconut-milk and shrimp broth, topped with bean sprouts, hard-boiled egg, celery, scallion, and fried shallot.

cover.altText: Mie celor, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Spanish dish made with stale bread and other ingredients, introduced by shepherds. It is popular across the Iberian Peninsula and the typical breakfast of hunters at monterías in some regions of Spain.

cover.altText: Migas, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: Fazer’s Mignon is an Easter chocolate egg with almond-hazelnut nougat filling inside a real eggshell. Introduced in 1896, it is the company’s second-oldest product.

cover.altText: Mignon: Partially peeled chocolate egg Mignon producted by Fazer

list.shortDescription: A Spanish cream-filled puff pastry dessert created by Manuel Blanco in Pamplona and associated with La Roda, Castilla–La Mancha. It took its name from Miguel, who received the first bite.

cover.altText: Miguelitos, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Macanese dish of beef or pork, minced or ground and stir-fried with onions, potatoes, and sometimes mushrooms, seasoned with Worcestershire sauce, molasses, and soy sauce. It is widely regarded as Macau's national dish.

cover.altText: Minchee: Minchee

list.shortDescription: A wild root from Tanzania’s Makonde Plateau, eaten as food and widely traded on the plateau and in nearby lowlands.

cover.altText: Ming'oko: Tanzanian vine (related to Dioscorea villosa) known as mtipu

list.shortDescription: Mititei are Romanian grilled ground-meat sausages made from beef, lamb, and pork, seasoned with garlic, black pepper, thyme, coriander, anise, savory, and sometimes paprika, with sodium bicarbonate and broth or water added.

cover.altText: Mititei: Mititei aufm Kohlegrill (18 Stück; ca. 1 kg rohes Hackfleisch)

list.shortDescription: A Hausa dish also known as moringa soup, made chiefly from the leaves of Moringa oleifera and combined with groundnut paste, ground tomato, beef, cubes, daddawa, and palm oil.

Pampangan glutinous rice balls made from galapong, filled with mung or red bean paste and shaped into balls or ovals. Boiled until they float, then topped with sesame seeds or crushed peanuts and served hot with sweetened coconut milk sauce.

cover.altText: Moche, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Andalusian bread with a white, floured crust and soft, easily crumbling crumb, made from hydrated, lightly kneaded dough and slow-baked. Served with olive oil, tomato, jamón serrano, or manteca colorá.

cover.altText: Mollete of Antequera: A typical food in South Spain called "Mollete" (bread and olive oil)

list.shortDescription: Milanese meatballs developed to use leftover beef and enriched with sausage, salami, liver, and mortadella. The mixture, with breadcrumbs, eggs, cheese, garlic or onion, and nutmeg, is shaped into balls and fried.

cover.altText: Mondeghili: Mondeghili, traditional fried beef and pork meatballs from Lombardy, Italy with thier typical form

list.shortDescription: Mondulkiri wild honey is gathered by Bunong hunters from giant honey bee nests in the province’s rainforests. It is an important commercial non-timber forest product for some Bunong people.

A Taiwanese method of preparing stir-fried noodle dishes, developed by a waishengren in the 1950s. Despite its name, it has no Mongolian influence and is cooked on a specialized circular flatiron grill, not over an open flame.

cover.altText: Mongolian barbecue: Mongolian barbeque

list.shortDescription: A Taiwanese dish of sliced beef, typically flank steak, made with onions and paired with scallions or mixed vegetables. Often nonspicy, it is served over steamed rice or, in the US, crispy fried cellophane noodles.

cover.altText: Mongolian beef, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An American ham and cheese sandwich dipped in egg and pan-fried, a variation of the French croque monsieur.

cover.altText: Monte Cristo sandwich: Green chile, turkey, pepper jack, sourdough, deep fried with powdered sugar and raspberry jam

list.shortDescription: A Montreal kosher-style deli meat made from beef brisket salted and cured with spices, allowed to absorb flavor for a week before hot smoking and final steaming.

cover.altText: Montreal-style smoked meat: Schwartz's smoked meat medium fat Montreal Quebec 2010

list.shortDescription: A branded ice cream flavor from Denali Flavors Inc., made by various companies: vanilla ice cream with peanut butter cups and Moose Tracks fudge.
A Japanese-style Chinese noodle dish in Morioka’s local cuisine, based on zhajiangmian introduced from China. It ranks among Morioka’s three great noodles, with reimen and wanko soba.

cover.altText: Morioka jajamen: Jajamen in Morioka, Iwate

list.shortDescription: A Cuban dish of black beans and white rice cooked together with onion, garlic, and red and green bell pepper in a sofrito. Its name pairs the dark beans (“Moros”) with the white rice (“Cristianos”).

cover.altText: Moros y Cristianos, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: Afrikaner or Cape Dutch sweet buns from South Africa’s wine-producing Western Cape, traditionally served with tea or coffee and sometimes dried into rusks.

cover.altText: Mosbolletjies: This is an image of food from

list.shortDescription: A sweet-and-salty Moroccan meat tajine pairing ras el hanout spices with honey, cinnamon, and almonds. Often made with lamb ritually sacrificed for Eid al-Adha.

cover.altText: Mrouzia, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Jewish soup of Algerian and Tunisian communities made with seasonal vegetables, lamb, and matzah, often eaten during feasts and Passover.

cover.altText: Msoki: Msuki

list.shortDescription: An Estonian stew of sauerkraut with lard, meat (mostly pork), and pearl barley, considered a national food. The barley is inexpensive, adds nutritional value, and changes the dish’s appearance.

cover.altText: Mulgikapsad: Mulgikapsad, an Estonian national food

list.shortDescription: A savoury, crunchy Indian snack common in Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha. It is called murkulu in Telangana, janthikalu in Andhra Pradesh, and mudku or murku in Odisha.

cover.altText: Murukku, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Neapolitan pastry shaped as a parallelogram, with a soft, spiced cake-like interior covered in chocolate and usually served at Christmas. Variants use white chocolate, icing sugar, or candied fruit.

cover.altText: Mustacciuoli: Mustacciuoli

list.shortDescription: A Georgian pork aspic combining two components processed differently, both marinated in wine vinegar with tarragon and basil. It has hot and cold versions; the cold dish is served the next day with green onions and herbs.
A Serbian stew in which cold leftover barbecued meat is cooked with vegetables; meats from different animals and varied cuts may be used. Its name derives from mućkati, “to shake, stir, or mix.”

cover.altText: Mućkalica: Mućkalica

list.shortDescription: A German cooked sausage made with pork, grain, apples, and raisins. Its dough of bacon, pig masks, pork rind, pork blood, and grated rye or wheat flour is boiled, then sliced and pan-fried; it resembles black pudding but has a fruity flavor.

cover.altText: Möpkenbrot, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian and Malay rice dish pairing a scoop of nasi putih with small portions of meats, vegetables, peanuts, eggs, and fried-shrimp krupuk. In Java, it is also called nasi rames or sega campur.

cover.altText: Nasi Campur, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian rice dish of steamed, spiced rice wrapped in banana leaves, tied with lidi semat and grilled over charcoal, giving the leaf a burnt aroma. Developed in the early 2000s, probably from nasi timbel.

cover.altText: Nasi bakar: Nasi bakar, a seasoned and spiced rice cooked (grilled) inside banana leaf, served with ayam goreng (fried chicken) with mushroom, vegetables, and spicy chilli sambal. Jakarta, Indonesia

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian rice specialty from Pati Regency, Central Java, pairing steamed rice with sliced beef in a rich, sweet, savoury, and spicy golden-brown soup.

cover.altText: Nasi gandul, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A Central Javanese rice dish from Solo, Indonesia, cooked in coconut milk with chicken broth, salam leaves, lemongrass, and spices, giving the rice a rich, aromatic, succulent taste.

cover.altText: Nasi liwet: Nasi Liwet, rice with rich coconut milk, chicken and egg, a specialty of Solo (Surakarta) city, Central Java

list.shortDescription: An Indonesian rice dish of the Betawi, Malay, and Peranakan cuisines, mixed with ulam including the leaves of pegagan, kemangi, Vietnamese mint, and torch ginger, and accompanied by assorted side dishes.

cover.altText: Nasi ulam, a photograph of the dish

list.shortDescription: A layered Portuguese dessert of whipped cream topped with egg cream over crumbled cookies. Its name means “cream of the sky,” and it resembles Spanish natillas.

cover.altText: Natas do Céu: Natas do Céu - deser kuchni portugalskiej

list.shortDescription: A Batak fish dish from North Sumatra, Indonesia, made with burned catfish, mujahir, carp, or other fish, served with chili sauce or coated in condiments and sauces.
A Kazakh or Kyrgyz drink of milk or broth with horse meat, salt, kashk, and grains, consumed at Nowruz for good luck as a symbol of wealth and richness in the coming year.

cover.altText: Ndolé: This is an image of food from

cover.altText: Neapolitan wafer: Waffle

cover.altText: Neccio, a photograph of the dish

An Iranian sweet resembling white jam but thicker, popular in Afghan, Tajik, and Uzbek cuisines and traditional among Bukharan Jews.

cover.altText: Nsala soup: White soup, Nsala soup

cover.altText: Nugatti, a photograph of the dish

cover.altText: Nutribun, a photograph of the dish

cover.altText: Nyama choma, a photograph of the dish

cover.altText: Ofada rice: This is an image of food from
