dish.longDescription: Nasi goreng is the Indonesian and Malay name for fried rice. The base preparation: pre-cooked rice stir-fried in a small amount of oil or margarine and seasoned with sweet soy sauce, shallots, garlic, ground shrimp paste, tamarind, and chilli. It is commonly served with additional ingredients — egg, chicken, prawns, vegetables. The dish is widely consumed across Maritime Southeast Asia, particularly in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, and southern Thailand, where it is part of daily meals, street-food culture, and festive cooking. Nasi goreng is distinguished from Chinese fried rice by its aromatic and smoky flavour from caramelised sweet soy sauce and powdered shrimp paste, and by being generally spicier. It is regarded as a national dish of Indonesia, and in Malaysia is officially recognised as part of the country's national culinary heritage.

dish.shortDescription: A mixed rice dish of layered basmati rice, marinated meat (typically chicken, mutton, or goat), fried onions, saffron, and whole spices. The Hyderabadi version is among the most famous.
dish.longDescription:
Hyderabadi biryani is a layered rice-and-meat dish from Hyderabad, in southern India. Unlike the Lucknowi style, where meat and rice are cooked separately before layering, the Hyderabadi method marinates the meat in yogurt and spices, partially cooks the basmati rice, then seals the pot with dough and slow-cooks over a low flame so the flavors steam together ("dum" cooking). The dish is traditionally made with goat, though chicken and vegetarian versions are common. Saffron, fried onions, mint, and whole spices like cardamom, cloves, and bay leaves give the rice its characteristic aroma and pale gold color.

The dish traces to the kitchens of the Nizam of Hyderabad, the princely rulers who patronized a hybrid cuisine blending Mughal Persian techniques with local Telugu and Deccani ingredients. Today it is served across South India, in Hyderabadi restaurants worldwide, and at weddings and Eid celebrations as a celebratory dish. The distinct accompaniments — mirchi ka salan (a tangy green-chili curry) and dahi chutney — are part of what defines "Hyderabadi" biryani specifically, rather than the broader Indian biryani family.

There are two main Hyderabadi styles: "kachi" biryani, where raw marinated meat is layered with par-cooked rice and cooked together (the more traditional method), and "pakki" biryani, where the meat is fully cooked before being layered with rice. The choice of fat is also a marker — some cooks insist on goat fat or ghee for the deep flavor it imparts. Today, Hyderabadi biryani is a protected geographical indication in India, and is widely considered one of the country's most distinctive regional rice dishes.

[Source: Wikipedia — Hyderabadi biryani, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyderabadi_biryani]

dish.shortDescription: Indonesian meatballs made from beef, chicken, or fish, served in a clear noodle soup with greens, tofu, fried shallots, and chili sauce.
dish.longDescription: Bakso is an Indonesian meatball or meat-paste soup. The meatball itself is made from beef surimi, with a texture comparable to the Chinese beef ball, fish ball, or pork ball. The word "bakso" may refer to a single meatball or to the complete dish of meatball soup. "Mie bakso" is the version served with yellow noodles and rice vermicelli; "bakso kuah" is the noodle-less soup. It is sold from street carts to high-end restaurants, and frozen bakso is sold in Indonesian supermarkets. The cited source lists it, alongside soto, satay, and siomay, as one of the most popular street foods in Indonesia.

dish.shortDescription: Palembang fish cakes made from ground mackerel or other white fish mixed with tapioca flour, formed into logs or balls, boiled, sliced, and fried, served with a sweet-sour-spicy cuko sauce.
dish.longDescription: Pempek, also called mpek-mpek or colloquially empek-empek, is a savoury Indonesian fishcake from Palembang, South Sumatra, made from fish and tapioca. The dish is served with a rich sweet-and-sour sauce called kuah cuka or kuah cuko, sometimes shortened to "cuko". Some Palembang residents also eat pempek with yellow noodles and diced cucumber to balance the vinegar's sourness, or add chilli powder to give the vinegar heat. The source identifies the regional name and the "cuko" dipping sauce as the main identifying features.

dish.shortDescription: A Goan curry of Portuguese origin: meat (traditionally pork) marinated in vinegar, garlic, and Kashmiri chili, then cooked with onions, ginger, and warm spices. The Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos became vindaloo over centuries.
dish.longDescription:
Vindaloo is a pungent, vinegar-based curry best known today in its British-Indian restaurant form, but its roots lie in colonial Goa. Portuguese settlers in the 15th century brought carne de vinha d'alhos — meat marinated in wine vinegar and garlic — to India's west coast, where local cooks adapted the recipe using palm vinegar and Kashmiri chilies. The name "vindaloo" comes from the Portuguese vinha d'alhos ("wine and garlic"). When the dish traveled to the UK with Goan migrants in the 19th and 20th centuries, it became a fixture of British curry houses, often served as the hottest item on the menu, far spicier than the Goan original.

Traditional Goan vindaloo is tangy rather than fiery, with pork as the most common meat, flavored with vinegar, garlic, ginger, cumin, mustard seeds, and a small amount of Kashmiri chili for color and warmth. The British restaurant version, popularised from the 1970s onward, typically uses more chili, sometimes tomato, and lamb or chicken. The dish is now common across South Asia, the UK, and globally in Indian restaurants, and remains closely associated with Goan Catholic cuisine.

In Goa itself, vindaloo is traditionally eaten with sannas (steamed rice cakes) or pão (Portuguese-influenced bread), and is considered a festive dish, especially around Christmas. The sharp vinegar-based marinade was originally a preservation technique, useful in a tropical climate before refrigeration. The dish's global reputation for extreme heat is, in large part, a British invention: restaurants used vindaloo as the "hottest curry" on their menus, and many diners ordered it as a test of fortitude, which encouraged ever-more-aggressive spicing in the restaurant version.

[Source: Wikipedia — Vindaloo, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vindaloo]

dish.shortDescription: An Indonesian salad of blanched and steamed vegetables, hard-boiled egg, fried tofu, and lontong, dressed in a peanut sauce sweetened with palm sugar and spiked with chili and tamarind.
dish.longDescription: Gado-gado is an Indonesian salad, in the Betawi and broader Indonesian sense, of raw, slightly boiled, blanched, or steamed vegetables together with hard-boiled eggs, boiled potato, fried tofu and tempeh, and sliced lontong (compressed rice cake wrapped in a banana leaf), dressed with a peanut sauce. In 2018, the Indonesian government promoted gado-gado as one of five national dishes of Indonesia, alongside soto, sate, nasi goreng, and rendang. The dish is Indonesian in its general form and specifically Betawi (the Jakarta region) in origin, and is found across the country with local variations.

dish.shortDescription: A thin, crispy South Indian crepe made from a fermented batter of rice and urad dal, served with coconut chutney and sambar. Sambar is closely related to the rasam and other lentil-stew traditions of the Deccan.
dish.longDescription:
A dosa (sometimes called dosai) is a thin, crisp pancake made from a fermented batter of rice and hulled black gram (urad dal). The batter is ground, salted, and left to ferment overnight, which produces the characteristic tangy flavor and the leavening that gives a well-made dosa its airy, lacy texture. The crepe is cooked on a flat iron griddle (tava) with ghee or oil, and is most associated with the states of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala in southern India.

Dosas are typically served with coconut chutney and sambar (a lentil-vegetable stew), and are eaten at any time of day, especially for breakfast. Plain dosas are called "paper" or "sada" dosa; stuffed versions, such as masala dosa filled with spiced potatoes, are enormously popular both in South India and abroad. South Indian restaurants outside India typically feature masala dosa as their signature dish. Fermentation makes dosas more digestible than other breads, and the dish is naturally gluten-free.

The fermentation process is the heart of a good dosa: long, slow fermentation produces a batter that is light, tangy, and crisp when cooked. Commercial and home cooks often add a small amount of fenugreek seeds or cooked rice to encourage wild yeasts. The dosa has been eaten in South India for centuries, with references in Tamil literature as far back as the 6th century, and is one of the oldest continuously prepared foods in the region. Today, both traditional and instant versions are popular across the world, and dosas are a defining dish of South Indian identity.

[Source: Wikipedia — Dosa (food), accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dosa_(food)]

dish.shortDescription: A Balinese whole-roasted suckling pig stuffed with a spice paste of turmeric, coriander, galangal, garlic, and chili, spit-roasted over coconut husk fire until the skin crackles.
dish.longDescription:
Babi guling is a Balinese whole-roasted pig. "Babi" means pig and "panggang" means grilled or roasted in Indonesian; "babi guling" is the more specific Balinese preparation, named for the turning of the spit. Outside Bali, the dish is uncommon, both because Indonesia is overwhelmingly Muslim and because the cooking technique — a whole young pig butterflied, spiced, and rotated slowly over coconut-wood embers — is uncommon outside Hindu-Balinese ceremonial contexts.

The cited source page is brief and does not document the ceremonial details or specific spice paste. A longer, dedicated treatment of the Balinese babi guling is not in the cited article.

The Balinese form, "nasi campur Bali", follows this template with a specifically Balinese choice of sides. dish.shortDescription: A South Asian savory fritter made from a ground legume or grain batter, shaped into rings or patties and fried until crisp outside and tender within.
dish.longDescription:
Vada is a broad category of savory, fried snacks from South India, typically made from a batter or dough of lentils, chickpeas, or other legumes, sometimes combined with vegetables and spices. The most common forms are medu vada (made from urad dal, shaped like a doughnut, and crisp outside with a soft interior), masala vada (a flatter, spiced chickpea-pea patty), and dahi vada (vadas soaked in yogurt and topped with chutneys). Vadas are typically served as breakfast or snack food, accompanied by coconut chutney and sambar.

The dish's roots are ancient: lentil-based fried foods similar to vada are mentioned in early Tamil and Sanskrit literature, and the term appears in South Indian texts dating back over a thousand years. Today vadas are sold by street vendors, served in restaurants, and made at home across South India, and have become familiar to international audiences through South Indian restaurants and diaspora communities. They are sometimes stuffed or topped with vegetables, peanuts, or coconut, reflecting regional variation.

The texture of a vada is its signature: crisp on the outside from a brief deep-frying, soft and airy on the inside from the fermented batter and the steam released during cooking. Medu vada — perhaps the most common form — is made from a wet batter of urad dal, green chilies, ginger, curry leaves, and black pepper, dropped by spoonful into hot oil. The batter is naturally light because the dal is ground to a fluffy, aerated paste. Vadas are sometimes served soaked (dahi vada), in a sambar (sambar vada), or as part of a thali. The dish is also a popular temple food, made as a daily offering in many South Indian Hindu temples.

[Source: Wikipedia — Vada (food), accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vada_(food)]

dish.shortDescription: A dry Indian curry of potatoes and cauliflower cooked with turmeric, cumin, ginger, garlic, and other regional spices.
dish.longDescription:
Aloo-gobi (also written aloo gobi or alu gobhi) is a dry vegetarian curry from the Indian subcontinent, made primarily with potatoes (aloo) and cauliflower (gobi) cooked with turmeric, cumin, coriander, ginger, garlic, and sometimes garam masala. The dish's signature yellow color comes from turmeric; the name "aloo-gobi" simply names its two main ingredients in Hindi-Urdu. It is one of the most common everyday vegetable dishes in North Indian and Pakistani home cooking, served with roti, paratha, or rice and dal.

dish.shortDescription: A crisp, triangular pastry filled with spiced potatoes, peas, lentils, meat, or vegetables and fried or baked across South Asia and its diaspora.
dish.longDescription:
A samosa is a fried or baked pastry turnover with a savory filling, most commonly a spiced mixture of mashed potatoes, peas, onions, and sometimes lentils or ground meat. The pastry is made from a simple flour-and-water (or flour-and-oil) dough, rolled thin, folded into a cone, stuffed, and sealed before being deep-fried until crisp and golden. The triangular or pyramidal shape is the most recognizable form, though regional variations include half-moon, cone, and tetrahedral shapes.

The dish's origins are not Indian: the word "samosa" derives from the Persian sanbosag (and ultimately from the even older Persian word sanbusa), and earlier forms of the stuffed pastry are documented in Central Asia and the Middle East from at least the 10th century. The samosa arrived in the Indian subcontinent by the 13th or 14th century through Persian-influenced courts and trade routes, and evolved into the spiced-potato version now associated with Indian street food. Today samosas are a staple across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and across South Asian and Middle Eastern diaspora communities, and are often served with mint or tamarind chutney.

The samosa's appeal is its portability, long shelf life, and the contrast between a crisp, oily shell and a savory, spice-laden interior. In South Asia, street vendors fold the dough and stuff the filling on site, then fry in large woks. In the Middle East, smaller versions known as sambousek or sambusa are popular, often filled with cheese or meat. The Indian diaspora has spread the samosa across the world, and it is today one of the most internationally recognizable Indian snacks, served at parties, sold in supermarkets, and adapted by chefs in countless regional styles.

[Source: Wikipedia — Samosa, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samosa]

dish.shortDescription: Soft, steamed South Indian cakes made from a fermented batter of rice and black gram, traditionally served with sambar and coconut or tomato chutney.
dish.longDescription:
Idli (or idly) is a soft, savory steamed cake made from a fermented batter of rice and hulled black lentils (urad dal). The batter is ground, salted, and fermented overnight, during which wild yeasts and lactobacilli produce a light, airy texture and a mildly tangy flavor. The batter is then poured into greased idli molds and steamed until pillowy and fully set. Idli is one of the most widely eaten breakfast foods across South India, where it is typically served with coconut chutney and sambar (a lentil-vegetable stew).

Idli's fermentation makes the starches more easily digestible, and the dish is naturally gluten-free, vegan, and low in fat — qualities that have made it popular in health-conscious and Indian-diaspora contexts worldwide. It is closely related to other fermented South Indian preparations like dosa and uttapam, all of which share a similar batter base. Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Andhra Pradesh each have their own regional variations, including rava idli (made with semolina) and thatte idli (plate idli, a Karnataka specialty).

The dish has ancient roots: lentil-and-rice fermented foods are mentioned in Tamil literature going back over a thousand years, and the modern idli as a steamed rice cake is documented in texts from the 12th century onward. Originally a temple and Brahmin food, idli spread across South India over the following centuries and is today one of the most universally recognized South Indian breakfasts. Its gentle flavor and easy digestibility make it a popular choice for travelers, the elderly, and the ill, and it is often recommended by doctors in South Asia as a recovery food.

[Source: Wikipedia — Idli, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idli]

dish.shortDescription: Roasted marinated chicken simmered in a smooth tomato, butter, and cream sauce seasoned with fenugreek and warm spices.
dish.longDescription:
Butter chicken (murgh makhani, "chicken with butter") is a North Indian curry of chicken cooked in a rich, creamy tomato-and-butter gravy. The sauce is built from tomato purée, butter (or ghee), cream, and cashew paste, seasoned with ginger, garlic, garam masala, fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi), and a touch of honey or sugar for sweetness. The result is a mild, velvety, deeply savory dish, typically orange-red in color.

The dish was invented in the 1950s at the Moti Mahal restaurant in Delhi, run by Kundan Lal Gujral and his family, who reportedly created it as a way to use up leftover tandoori chicken by simmering it in a rich tomato-cream sauce. It became a worldwide phenomenon partly through the spread of Punjabi cuisine, and is often cited (along with chicken tikka masala) as one of the most internationally recognized Indian dishes. Today it is a staple of Indian restaurants globally and a beloved comfort food across South Asia.

The dish's signature richness comes from a combination of butter and cream added near the end of cooking, which gives the sauce a velvety mouthfeel without the sharpness of tomato or the heaviness of straight cream. A pinch of kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) added at the end provides an earthy, slightly bitter aroma that balances the sweetness. Butter chicken is typically eaten with naan, roti, or jeera rice, and is often ordered alongside dal makhani at Indian restaurants to provide a creamy, tomato-rich contrast. It is sometimes called the "national dish of India" in informal polls, reflecting its popularity both domestically and abroad.

[Source: Wikipedia — Butter chicken, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butter_chicken]

dish.shortDescription: A North Indian combination of spiced chickpea curry and bhature, a large, leavened, deep-fried bread served hot with pickles, onion, and chutney.
dish.longDescription:
Chole-bhature is a North Indian dish pairing a spiced chickpea curry (chole or chana masala) with bhatura, a deep-fried leavened flatbread made from maida (refined wheat flour), yogurt, and a little baking soda. The combination is a classic Punjabi breakfast or lunch, often served with sliced onions, green chilies, and a wedge of lemon. The contrast of the fluffy, slightly sour, oily bread with the warm, earthy chickpea curry is the appeal.

Chickpea curries of this style have Mughal-era roots, with similar dishes found across North India, Pakistan, and the diaspora. The combination with bhatura, which originated in Punjab, gave the dish its modern identity, and it is now a fixture of street food stalls, dhabas, and family kitchens across the region. In Delhi and surrounding states, chole-bhature is a popular weekend breakfast, often served in large portions at roadside eateries that specialize in it.

The chickpea curry is flavored with a base of onion, tomato, ginger, garlic, and a warming blend of spices that typically includes cumin, coriander, amchur (dried mango powder), garam masala, and sometimes anardana (dried pomegranate seeds). The chickpeas are usually cooked until very soft, so the gravy is thick and rich. Bhatura, by contrast, is quick to make — the dough is allowed to rise briefly, then shaped into small ovals and deep-fried until puffed and blistered. The combination is a popular celebratory dish, often served at weddings, festivals, and Sunday family meals across the Punjab and Delhi.

[Source: Wikipedia — Chole bhature, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chole_bhature]

dish.shortDescription: A thin, crisp South Indian fermented rice-and-lentil crepe filled with a fragrant potato masala and served with sambar and chutney.
dish.longDescription:
Masala dosa is a crisp South Indian crepe made from a fermented rice-and-lentil batter, stuffed with a spiced potato-and-onion filling. The dosa itself is golden and lacy, spread thin on a hot griddle with ghee or oil, while the filling — known as "aloo bhaji" or "masala" — is a fragrant mixture of boiled potatoes, mustard seeds, cumin, turmeric, curry leaves, ginger, and green chilies, often finished with fresh coriander and a squeeze of lemon.

The dish is most strongly associated with Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and is one of the most widely consumed breakfast items in South India, found in udupi restaurants, darshinis, and street stalls across cities like Bangalore, Chennai, and Mangalore. It is also one of the most internationally recognizable South Indian dishes, served in Indian restaurants worldwide. The combination of the tangy, crisp crepe with the soft, spiced potato filling is what makes masala dosa distinct from plain dosa or other stuffed variants.

The potato filling is the heart of the dish: potatoes are boiled, cubed, and tossed with tempered spices (mustard seeds, urad dal, curry leaves, dried red chilies) and aromatics like ginger, green chili, and onion. A squeeze of lemon and a handful of fresh coriander finish the filling with brightness. The dosa itself is made from the same rice-and-urad-dal batter as plain dosa, fermented overnight for a tangy flavor, and spread thin on a hot tava with ghee. Together, the contrast of textures and flavors — crisp and soft, tangy and savory, slightly sweet and slightly spicy — defines the dish.

[Source: Wikipedia — Masala dosa, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masala_dosa]

dish.shortDescription: Cubes of fresh paneer cheese served in a smooth spinach sauce seasoned with ginger, garlic, green chili, and warming spices.
dish.longDescription:
Palak paneer is a North Indian curry of paneer (a fresh, non-melting Indian cheese) in a thick, smooth gravy made from puréed spinach (palak in Hindi). The spinach is blanched and blended with onion, tomato, ginger, garlic, and green chili, then simmered with cubed paneer, cream or butter, and finishing spices such as garam masala and kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves). The result is a deep green, mildly spiced, creamy dish that pairs especially well with roti, naan, or jeera rice.

Palak paneer is a staple of Punjabi cuisine and is widely served in Indian restaurants globally. The dish is closely related to saag paneer, which uses a mixture of slow-cooked greens rather than just spinach, and to palak chhena, the Eastern-Indian variant that uses chhena (a softer, crumblier fresh cheese) instead of paneer. A vegetarian staple, palak paneer is a popular source of protein, calcium, and iron in vegetarian Indian diets.

The vivid green color of the gravy comes from fresh spinach, ideally blanched briefly to set the color before being puréed. A pinch of kasuri methi added at the end provides an earthy, slightly bitter aroma that is characteristic of the dish and distinguishes it from a generic spinach curry. Paneer, the cheese, is made by curdling milk with lemon juice or vinegar, then draining and pressing the curds; it holds its shape during cooking and provides a chewy, mild counterpoint to the rich gravy. The dish is sometimes made with spinach alone and sometimes with a blend of spinach and other greens such as mustard greens or fenugreek, depending on the region and the cook.

[Source: Wikipedia — Palak paneer, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palak_paneer]

The spinach is blanched and blended with onion, tomato, ginger, garlic, and green chili, then simmered with cubed paneer, cream or butter, and finishing spices such as garam masala and kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves).
The result is a deep green, mildly spiced, creamy dish that pairs especially well with roti, naan, or jeera rice.
Palak paneer is a staple of Punjabi cuisine and is widely served in Indian restaurants globally.

The dish is closely related to saag paneer, which uses a mixture of slow-cooked greens rather than just spinach, and to palak chhena, the Eastern-Indian variant that uses chhena (a softer, crumblier fresh cheese) instead of paneer.
A vegetarian staple, palak paneer is a popular source of protein, calcium, and iron in vegetarian Indian diets.
The vivid green color of the gravy comes from fresh spinach, ideally blanched briefly to set the color before being puréed.
A pinch of kasuri methi added at the end provides an earthy, slightly bitter aroma that is characteristic of the dish and distinguishes it from a generic spinach curry.

Paneer, the cheese, is made by curdling milk with lemon juice or vinegar, then draining and pressing the curds; it holds its shape during cooking and provides a chewy, mild counterpoint to the rich gravy.
The dish is sometimes made with spinach alone and sometimes with a blend of spinach and other greens such as mustard greens or fenugreek, depending on the region and the cook.
[Source: Wikipedia — Palak paneer, accessed 2026-10-17, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palak_paneer]

dish.shortDescription: An Indonesian chicken rice porridge topped with shredded chicken, scallions, fried shallots, crackers, soy sauce, and sometimes a soft-boiled egg.
dish.longDescription: Bubur ayam is the Indonesian and Malay name for chicken congee: rice porridge with shredded chicken, served with condiments including chopped scallion, crispy fried shallot, celery, preserved vegetables (tongcay or chai poh), fried soybean, crullers (youtiao, locally called cakwe), salty and sweet soy sauce, and sometimes a yellow chicken broth poured over the top, with kerupuk (Indonesian crackers) on the side. Unlike many Indonesian dishes, the porridge itself is not spicy; sambal is served separately for those who want heat. It is sold from travelling carts in residential streets in the morning, from warung, from fast-food chains, and from five-star hotel restaurants.

dish.shortDescription: Indonesian grilled fish rubbed with a sweet-spicy spice paste, cooked over charcoal, and served with sambal, lime, and rice.
dish.longDescription: Ikan bakar is the Indonesian and Malay name for charcoal-grilled fish or other seafood; the term literally means "grilled fish" in both languages. The dish differs from other grilled-fish preparations in the seasonings used: a flavouring paste (bumbu), sweet soy sauce (kecap manis), and sambal, with the fish wrapped in a banana leaf and cooked on a charcoal fire. The dish is found across Indonesia and Malaysia.

dish.shortDescription: An Indonesian stuffed pancake with savory egg, meat, and scallion fillings or a thick sweet version layered with chocolate, peanuts, cheese, or condensed milk.
dish.longDescription: In Indonesia, "martabak" refers to two distinct dishes. Martabak manis is a thick sweet folded pancake based on apam balik, layered with chocolate, cheese, or sugar. Martabak telur is a pan-fried crepe folded around beaten egg, chopped leeks or scallions, and minced meat, then cut into squares and eaten with curry, pickles, or chilli sauce; it is the closer Indonesian relative of murtabak. The name "murtabak" comes from the Arabic mutabbaq, meaning "folded", and the dish is shared across the Arabian Peninsula, the Indian subcontinent, and Maritime Southeast Asia. A thinner, drier variant of martabak manis is called martabak tipis kering.

dish.shortDescription: A Minangkabau rice meal served with an assortment of rich curries, vegetables, sambal, and meat or fish dishes, named for the city of Padang.
dish.longDescription: Nasi padang is a Minangkabau rice meal of steamed white rice served with a choice of pre-cooked dishes from West Sumatra, Indonesia, named for the city of Padang. The cited source calls it "a miniature banquet of meats, fish, vegetables, and spicy sambals eaten with plain white rice", and identifies it as Sumatra's most famous food export and the Minangkabau people's primary contribution to Indonesian cuisine. Padang restaurants are recognisable by their Rumah Gadang-style facades and the stacked rows of bowls visible through the window. Smaller Padang restaurants often carry Minang-language names. The dish is found across Sumatra, Java, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Nusa Tenggara, Papua, and in neighbouring countries including Malaysia, Singapore, East Timor, and Australia.

dish.shortDescription: A Nigerian cassava food of the Igbos, made by peeling, washing, cooking, slicing, and soaking cassava for a day. Shredded dried cassava is softened in boiled water and covered for a few minutes.
dish.longDescription: Abacha is a product of cassava tubers. When the processing of it is done from scratch, harvested cassava is obtained, peeled, washed, cooked and sliced into desired sizes or shapes. It is soaked for a day. It could be prepared instantly as abacha or sun-dried for future use. Shredded dried cassava first needs to be softened by soaking in boiled water and covered up for a few minutes. Abacha is quite different from mpataka. Mpataka is a cassava snack made by boiling the cassava, cutting it into smaller pieces and soaking it in running water for 12–36 hours. It is eaten with akị bekee, ube and ube ọkpoko. In some places across Igboland, mpataka is also called abacha mmiri, eberebe or jigbo, iboh or iwakpu.

dish.shortDescription: A palm-fruit soup of the Ibibio people in Akwa Ibom and the Urhobo and Isoko people in Delta State, made with palm pulp, atama leaf, salt, pepper, and chosen proteins.
dish.longDescription: It is a popular food among the Delta, Cross River and Akwa Ibom State people of Nigeria. The Urhobo people of Delta state called it amme-edi or banga soup. The soup is made from palm fruit-pulp that is derived from palm fruit; the extracted palm-pulp is base primary ingredient for the soup. Atama soup is thick and dark brown in color. It is normally prepared with Atama leaf, choice of protein like fresh meat or dry meat(mostly bush meat), dry fish, fresh fish and sometimes shrimp(dry or fresh), periwinkle as added proteins for more enhanced flavor. Ingredients: primary ingredients are Fresh Atama leaf,fresh palm-pulp sourced from palm fruit, salt and pepper and secondary ingredients which are decided based on preference of the cooker are onions, salt, pepper(different kinds of pepper are preferences) and different kinds of spices could be added depending on the cooker preferred or desired taste or flavor. This soup could be styled into different flavors depending on cooking preferences. Every added ingredient could drastically change the taste of the food.
dish.name: Atama soup
dish.description: A palm-fruit soup of the Ibibio people in Akwa Ibom and the Urhobo and Isoko people in Delta State, made with palm pulp, atama leaf, salt, pepper, and chosen proteins.

Saying something is an avial is also a common phrase attributing that thing to being a mess.

dish.shortDescription: A Portuguese oven-baked cod dish layered with onion, mashed potatoes seasoned with ground nutmeg, and mayonnaise. Created in Porto by Zé do Pipo, it is usually garnished with olives or peppers.
dish.longDescription: It is an oven baked dish, consisting in layers of bacalhau, onion, mashed potatoes with a hint of ground nutmeg, and mayonnaise. Although mayonnaise is not traditionally used in Portuguese cuisine, in this dish it's considered typical. It is usually garnished with olives or peppers. The recipe originates from Porto, having achieved popularity in Vizela, being named after its creator, Zé do Pipo, who owned a famous restaurant in Porto during the 1960s. He won a national gastronomic contest with this main course, making many restaurants adopt it in their menus and popularizing it through the country to this day.

dish.shortDescription: Yellowish tofu-skin sheets made from soybeans form when a protein-lipid film develops on soy milk heated to 80–90°C. The films are collected and dried; without coagulant, they are not technically tofu.
dish.longDescription: During the boiling of soy milk, typically heated to 80–90 °C, in an open shallow pan, a film or skin composed primarily of a soy protein-lipid complex forms on the liquid surface. The films are collected and dried into yellowish sheets known as tofu skin. Since tofu skin is not produced using a coagulant, it is not technically a proper tofu; however, it does have a similar texture and flavor to some tofu products.

dish.shortDescription: A dessert of ice cream in a pie dish, lined with slices of sponge cake or Christmas pudding and topped with meringue, then briefly baked or torched until the meringue browns without the ice cream melting.
dish.longDescription: The dish is made of ice cream placed in a pie dish, lined with slices of sponge cake or Christmas pudding, and topped with meringue. After having been placed in the freezer, the entire dessert is then placed in an extremely hot oven for a brief time, long enough to firm and caramelize the meringue but not long enough to begin melting the ice cream. Another common method of browning the meringue is to torch the dessert, sometimes even setting it on fire for presentational purposes.

dish.longDescription: Traditionally, its preparation and consumption were an important economizing custom, especially for the rural poor. Particularly, it allowed farmers to use various less-desirable parts of pork, which were made more palatable by being added to a seasoned porridge of groats or flour. The closely related 'Panhas', 'Pannas' or 'Möppkenbrot' are widely known in the whole northwest of Germany; the last variety is a speciality of middle Westphalia and Rhineland.

dish.shortDescription: An Albanian cookie from Elbasan made with butter, sugar, eggs, and corn flour, kneaded in a copper bowl. It is traditionally eaten on Dita e Verës on 14 March.
dish.longDescription: It is traditionally eaten on Dita e Verës, an Albanian pagan holiday celebrated on 14 March. It is sometimes called kulaç me finj, as it may optionally contain finj, a mixture of ashes from a wood stove boiled in water. It consists of butter, sugar, eggs, and corn flour. It is traditionally kneaded in a copper bowl, which is supposed to improve the texture of the dough. The dough must be kneaded vigorously, which is why the men of the house are often involved in the ballokume preparation.

dish.shortDescription: Mexican street food of sliced, spit-grilled meat, usually pork, seasoned with traditional Mexican adobada marinade. It is especially prominent in Puebla and also called taco de trompo or taco de adobada in parts of northern and coastal Mexico.
dish.longDescription: The method of preparing and cooking al pastor is based on the lamb shawarma brought by Lebanese immigrants to the region. Al pastor features a flavor palette that uses traditional Mexican adobada (marinade). It is a popular street food that has spread to the United States. In some places of northern Mexico and coastal Mexico, such as in Baja California, taco al pastor is known as taco de trompo or taco de adobada.

dish.shortDescription: A Nigerian jelly-like staple made with corn flour and water, prepared similarly to pap and popular in Southern and parts of Northern Nigeria. Agidi Jollof is prepared like Jollof rice.
dish.longDescription: It is mostly popular among people of Southern and parts of Northern Nigeria. The Ngwa Igbos refer to it as Àsụrụàsụ Oka, Nri Oka, or Agidi (Igbo), Eko/Agidi(Yoruba), Akasan(Benin), Komu(Hausa), Kafa(Ghana), Akwapim (Togo). It is often described as a Nigerian jelly-like dish and is made in a way similar to pap. Agidi also has a variant known as “Agidi Jollof,” which is prepared similarly to Jollof rice. Agidi Jollof is most similar to the mesoamerican tamale dish. It is made with corn flour and water.

dish.shortDescription: A Nigerian swallow food of the Yoruba in southwestern Nigeria, made from yam, cassava flour, or unripe plantain flour. Yam tubers are peeled, sliced, dried, and ground; it is served with ewédú, gbẹ̀gìrì, or soups.
dish.longDescription: It is made of yam, cassava flour, or unripe plantain flour. Tubers of yams are peeled, sliced, cleaned, dried and then ground into flour. It is also called èlùbọ́. Yams are white in colour but turn brown when dried which gives àmàlà its colour. It is a popular side dish served with ewédú and gbẹ̀gìrì, but it is also served with a variety of other ọbè (soups), such as ẹ̀fọ́, ilá, and ogbono.
dish.name: amala
dish.description: A Nigerian swallow food of the Yoruba in southwestern Nigeria, made from yam, cassava flour, or unripe plantain flour. Yam tubers are peeled, sliced, dried, and ground; it is served with ewédú, gbẹ̀gìrì, or soups.

dish.shortDescription: Indonesian vegetable fritters, or gorengan, made with bean sprouts, shredded cabbage, and carrots in a batter of flour, corn starch, and sago or tapioca, then deep-fried in cooking oil for a crisp texture.
dish.longDescription: Bakwan are usually sold by traveling street vendors. The ingredients are vegetables—usually bean sprouts, shredded cabbage and carrots—battered and deep-fried in cooking oil. To achieve a crispy texture, the batter uses a mixture of flour, corn starch and sago or tapioca. In West Java bakwan is known as bala-bala and in Semarang is called badak. It is similar to Japanese yasai tenpura, Korean pajeon, Bruneian cucur, Indian pakora, Burmese a-kyaw, Caribbean pholourie or Filipino ukoy.
dish.name: bakwan
dish.description: Indonesian vegetable fritters, or gorengan, made with bean sprouts, shredded cabbage, and carrots in a batter of flour, corn starch, and sago or tapioca, then deep-fried in cooking oil for a crisp texture.

dish.longDescription: It is a fried batter soaked in syrup, similar to jalebis or churros. It is made from unleavened choux pastry dough, usually about 3 inches long, piped with a pastry bag using an open star or similar tip. It is first deep-fried to golden colour and then sugar-sweet syrup is poured over it when still hot.

dish.description: A deep-fried dessert across Egypt, the Levant, Greece, and former Ottoman regional cuisines, made from piped unleavened choux pastry and drenched in sweet syrup while hot.

Types of almond biscuits include almond macaroons, Italian amaretti, Spanish almendrados, Armenian nshablits, qurabiya, and Moroccan biscuits and desserts. In addition, Turkish şekerpare are often decorated with an almond.

It is often served as halves, with the inside slightly carved out. The dish is eaten warm and cold throughout Turkey, particularly during wintertime.

It is also one of the more traditional Palestinian desserts and it is easy to find stalls selling barazek on the streets of Jerusalem.

They are often eaten as a breakfast food; toppings vary from whipped cream, confectioners' sugar, soft fruit, and chocolate spread, to syrup and butter or margarine. They may also be served with vanilla ice cream and fresh fruit as a dessert.

dish.longDescription: It is made from glutinous rice (diket) that is pounded into a paste, wrapped in banana or rattan leaves, and steamed. Variants may also add sesame seeds or sweet potato. They are popularly eaten on special occasions or as a snack. Uncooked binakle, along with rice wine (baya), are common offerings to the bulul ancestor spirits in Ifugao rituals.

dish.shortDescription: An Indonesian black rice pudding made by boiling glutinous rice until soft, then adding coconut milk and palm or cane sugar. It is served as a dessert, snack, or breakfast.
dish.longDescription: The black glutinous rice are boiled until soft, and sugar and coconut milk are added. It is often described as "black glutinous rice pudding" and is very similar to black rice tong sui made from black rice. It is often served as dessert or snack, for supper, for tea time, any time of the day; however, it is a popular choice for breakfast for those who prefer sweet treats instead of its savory counterpart bubur ayam.
dish.name: Bubur ketan hitam
dish.description: An Indonesian black rice pudding made by boiling glutinous rice until soft, then adding coconut milk and palm or cane sugar. It is served as a dessert, snack, or breakfast.

dish.shortDescription: A Hanoi dish of grilled fatty pork served over white rice noodles with herbs and a dipping sauce. It was described by Vietnamese food writer Vũ Bằng in 1959.
dish.longDescription: Bún chả is served with grilled fatty pork (chả) over a plate of white rice noodles (bún) and herbs with a side dish of dipping sauce. The dish was described in 1959 by Vietnamese food writer Vũ Bằng (1913–1984), who described Hanoi as a town "transfixed by bún chả". Hanoi's first bún chả restaurant was on Gia Ngư, Hoàn Kiếm District, in Hanoi's Old Quarter.

dish.description: A Hanoi dish of grilled fatty pork served over white rice noodles with herbs and a dipping sauce. It was described by Vietnamese food writer Vũ Bằng in 1959.

Crab jujube is a popular dish among Thai Chinese people in Thailand where it is known as hoicho.

dish.longDescription: Sugar pieces are flavoured with orange, lemon, vanilla, or almond essence, then inserted into the dough before cooking. They melt and cool, leaving gaps encrusted in sugar. The craquelin dough will have a viennoiserie dough overlay to prevent sugar protrusion.

dish.longDescription: Ingredients include pasta, crawfish tail meat, onion, garlic, creole seasoning, cream, wine, salt, pepper, and butter. The dish was created by chef Pierre Hilzim who is the head of Kajun Kettle Foods. He named it after his wife Monica Davidson. Parsley can be used as a garnish. Shrimp, crabmeat and oysters can be substituted for crawfish.
dish.name: Crawfish Monica

This monastery was located next to the Church of Santa Croce, from which these sweet pastries take their name.

dish.shortDescription: A Sicilian porridge of boiled wheatberries and sugar, eaten on December 13 for Saint Lucy’s feast. It commemorates Sicily’s relief from a food shortage and the arrival of wheat in Palermo in 1646.
dish.longDescription: The dish is consumed in Sicily and in isolated pockets of southern Italy, as well as their communities abroad. It commemorates the relief from a food shortage in Sicily and the unexpected arrival of a cargo of wheat, which tradition says arrived in the port of Palermo on Saint Lucy's Feast in 1646. According to custom, bread should not be eaten on December 13; cuccìa should be the only source of wheat, and the primary source of nourishment for the day.

dish.description: A Sicilian porridge of boiled wheatberries and sugar, eaten on December 13 for Saint Lucy’s feast. It commemorates Sicily’s relief from a food shortage and the arrival of wheat in Palermo in 1646.

dish.shortDescription: A South Asian meal of thick lentil soup, dal, paired with cooked rice, bhat. A daily staple in South Asia and the Caribbean, providing protein and carbohydrates.
dish.longDescription: It is a traditional meal in South Asia and one of the most common everyday meals in the region and in the Caribbean. The meal is simple, nutritious, and widely eaten as a daily staple food. The combination of dal and bhat is valued because it provides both protein and carbohydrates, making it a balanced and filling meal.
dish.name: Dal bhat
dish.description: A South Asian meal of thick lentil soup, dal, paired with cooked rice, bhat. A daily staple in South Asia and the Caribbean, providing protein and carbohydrates.

dish.shortDescription: A South Asian puri made from whole-wheat flour, deep-fried and filled with chickpea or lentil dal. Caribbean and Mauritian variants use white flour, are griddle-baked on a tava, and commonly contain split peas.
dish.longDescription: The South Asian version is a type of puri, a deep-fried flatbread made of whole wheat flour, and uses dal made of chickpeas or lentils. Its variants are dhalpuri roti in Caribbean cuisine and dholl puri in Mauritian cuisine, both of which instead use white flour and are griddle-baked on a tava. Split peas are a common filling for both variants. Dhalpuri and dholl puri are both wrapped around curry as sandwiches and served as street food.
dish.name: Dalpuri
dish.description: A South Asian puri made from whole-wheat flour, deep-fried and filled with chickpea or lentil dal. Caribbean and Mauritian variants use white flour, are griddle-baked on a tava, and commonly contain split peas.

dish.longDescription: In Germany and in Switzerland, the same type of dessert is known as a Coupe Dänemark. The dessert is similar to the American sundae. The dish that was created by Auguste Escoffier originally consisted of almond milk ice cream, poached peach, lemon sorbet and white currants.

dish.shortDescription: A Taiwanese breakfast of thin dough kneaded from flour, potato starch, glutinous rice flour, and water, topped with a baked omelet. Regional recipes vary, and it is sold at breakfast shops, restaurants, night markets, and supermarkets.
dish.longDescription: Different regions make the dish differently, in most cases, the dough is made by kneading flour, potato starch, glutinous rice flour, and water into a thin dough, and an omelet is baked on top of the dough. In Taiwan, dan bing is mainly sold at breakfast shops, restaurants as well as night market food stalls. They are also sold commercially in supermarkets, where the dough is frozen in plastic packaging, and egg is added as the dough is heated.
dish.name: Danbing
dish.description: A Taiwanese breakfast of thin dough kneaded from flour, potato starch, glutinous rice flour, and water, topped with a baked omelet. Regional recipes vary, and it is sold at breakfast shops, restaurants, night markets, and supermarkets.

dish.shortDescription: A Tausug Filipino dessert of crêpes made with ground glutinous rice and coconut milk, rolled around sweetened coconut meat and sometimes flavored with pandan leaves.
dish.longDescription: It originates from the Tausug people of the Philippines. It is also known as balolon among the Maranao people. The crêpe wrapper is similar to the lumpia wrapper, except that it uses batter made from unsweetened ground glutinous rice with coconut milk (galapong). The wrap is sometimes flavored with pandan leaves. However, modern versions can use flour.
dish.name: Daral
dish.description: A Tausug Filipino dessert of crêpes made with ground glutinous rice and coconut milk, rolled around sweetened coconut meat and sometimes flavored with pandan leaves.

dish.shortDescription: A Batak fish dish from North Sumatra, Indonesia, made with raw carp soaked in Kaffir limes and seasoned with andaliman. Its Toba Batak name means “pickled fish.”
dish.longDescription: The name of the dish means "pickled fish" in the Toba Batak language. The dish is made with raw carp which is soaked in Kaffir limes and seasoned with andaliman. According to local oral tradition, only Batak kings were allowed to eat the dish, but in modern times there is no such restriction.
dish.name: Dengke Mas Naniura
dish.description: A Batak fish dish from North Sumatra, Indonesia, made with raw carp soaked in Kaffir limes and seasoned with andaliman. Its Toba Batak name means “pickled fish.”

dish.shortDescription: An American pie made with butter, sugar, eggs, and flour, using available ingredients when seasonal or costly ones were lacking. It was common before refrigeration and canned fillings, notably during the Great Depression and World War II rationing.
dish.longDescription: These pies were more common before refrigeration and canned pie fillings, and during times of hardship like the Great Depression and rationing of World War II.
dish.name: Desperation pie
dish.description: An American pie made with butter, sugar, eggs, and flour, using available ingredients when seasonal or costly ones were lacking. It was common before refrigeration and canned fillings, notably during the Great Depression and World War II rationing.

Dibi is commonly served by street vendors in Mali and Senegal. Many dibiteries in Senegal's capital city of Dakar are run by foreigners, particularly from the Hausa people of Nigeria. "Dibi" is a Soninke word that refers to barbecue.

dish.longDescription: Edikang ikong is a nutritious soup and expensive to prepare, and has been described as being mostly eaten by rich people in Nigeria. Ingredients used in edikang ikong include beef and dried fish, bush meat, crayfish, shaki, kanda, pumpkin leaves, water leaves, ikong ubong, onion, periwinkle, palm oil, salt and pepper.

dish.longDescription: It is popularly known amongst the Cross River State people and Akwaibom State people. The soup is made from Editan leaf, a bitter leaf. Before being cooked the bitterness must be squeezed out.
dish.name: Editan
dish.description: A Nigerian vegetable soup of the Efik people in Cross River State, made from bitter Editan leaves that are squeezed to remove bitterness before cooking. It is also popular in Akwa Ibom State.

dish.shortDescription: A Yoruba vegetable soup from South West Nigeria, traditionally prepared with locally grown vegetables, meat, fish, and spices. Common additions include spinach, pumpkin leaves, sorrel leaves, peppers, and onions.
dish.longDescription: The two vegetables most commonly used to prepare the soup are Celosia argentea and Amaranthus hybridus. The history of Efo riro is deeply rooted in the Yoruba culture. It was traditionally prepared with the locally grown vegetables, meat, fish, and a mixture of spices. The choice of vegetables and proteins varies based on personal preference and regional availability. The most commonly used vegetables are spinach, pumpkin leaves, or sorrel leaves, often combined with bell peppers, chili peppers, and onions.
dish.name: Efo riro
dish.description: A Yoruba vegetable soup from South West Nigeria, traditionally prepared with locally grown vegetables, meat, fish, and spices. Common additions include spinach, pumpkin leaves, sorrel leaves, peppers, and onions.

dish.shortDescription: A Turkish pudding of kadayıf made with ekmek, usually served with kaymak, a clotted cream. Historically a specialty of Afyonkarahisar, it is served at special events there and may be flavored or topped with cherries.
dish.longDescription: The Turkish name of the dessert literally translates as "Kadayıf made of ekmek " giving clues on its preparation. The dessert is usually served with kaymak, a kind of clotted cream. Historically being a regional specialty of Afyonkarahisar, the dessert is served in special events within its region of origin. The dessert may optionally be flavored or topped with cherries of which Afyonkarahisar produces a significant amount. In Greek cuisine, it is known as "ekmek kataifi".

dish.shortDescription: A Mexican dish of corn tortillas rolled around a filling and covered in refried bean sauce, typically served with cheese, onions, and crema. Often eaten at breakfast, with regional recipe variations.
dish.longDescription: They are similar to enchiladas, but are prepared using a sauce made from refried beans rather than chili peppers. Enfrijoladas are typically served with cheese, onions, and crema. There are regional differences to the recipe, and it is also eaten in some parts of Central America. In Mexico, Enfrijoladas is often served as a breakfast dish.

dish.shortDescription: A common Chadian dish of boiled flour, typically served with moulah sauce. It is a staple eaten throughout Chad, often for lunch and dinner, and is also called gou in Zaghawa and tii in Dazaga.
dish.longDescription: Esh is a staple food of Chad and is often eaten daily for lunch and dinner. It is consumed throughout Chad and is known by different names such as gou in Zaghawa and tii in Dazaga.
dish.name: Esh
dish.description: A common Chadian dish of boiled flour, typically served with moulah sauce. It is a staple eaten throughout Chad, often for lunch and dinner, and is also called gou in Zaghawa and tii in Dazaga.

dish.shortDescription: A traditional Catalan salad of shredded salt cod, tomatoes, onions, olive oil, vinegar, and salt, sometimes garnished with olives or hard-boiled eggs. It is popular in warm weather and often served as tapas.
dish.longDescription: Specific recipes vary, with some including ingredients such as eggplant and bell peppers. Esqueixada is particularly popular in warm weather and is sometimes considered a summertime dish. It is often served as a tapas dish.
dish.name: Esqueixada

dish.longDescription: The dessert was traditionally given by a suitor but is now part of many wedding banquets. It is traditional for a bridegroom to send bánh phu thê to the bride on the couple's wedding day to symbolize wishes for a happy future.

dish.shortDescription: Thin round breads from Italy’s Apennines near Modena, made with flour, water, salt and yeast. They can be filled with pork-lard cunza flavored with garlic and rosemary, cold cuts, cheese, or sweet spreads.
dish.longDescription: They are made with flour, water, salt, and yeast, and traditionally eaten filled with cunza, a spread made from pork lard and flavoured with garlic and rosemary or with cold cuts, boar, rabbit, cheese, salty dressings or sweet spreads. In the Apennines, crescente have long been eaten at home or enjoyed in traditional restaurants, but in the last decade some fast food and casual restaurants have added crescente to their menus. Similar breads such as piadina, borlengo, gnocco fritto, and panigaccio are made in neighbouring areas.
dish.name: Tigella

dish.shortDescription: A Libyan unleavened bread made by boiling barley or wheat flour in water, beating the dough with a magraf, then baking or steaming it in a pan.
dish.longDescription: Bazin is prepared by boiling barley flour or wheat flour in water and then beating it to create a dough using a magraf, which is a unique stick designed for this purpose. The dough may then be placed in a pan and allowed time to harden, after which it is baked or steamed. The salt contributes to the hardness of the bazin. Bazin may have a paste-like and hardened texture. It may also be prepared using whole wheat flour, olive oil, honey and/or pepper as ingredients.
dish.name: bazeen
dish.description: A Libyan unleavened bread made by boiling barley or wheat flour in water, beating the dough with a magraf, then baking or steaming it in a pan.

dish.longDescription: It has become a traditional Cape Malay sweet, milk drink, made with vermicelli, sago, sugar, and flavoured with cardamom, stick cinnamon, and rose water. dish.shortDescription: An Algerian pastry of thin “dyoul” sheets filled with mashed potatoes, chopped onions, cumin and paprika. Folded into triangles, rectangles or spirals, it is baked or deep-fried until golden and crispy.
dish.longDescription: Algerian bourek is usually made up of thin pastry sheets, known as "dyoul" in Algeria, which can be purchased from stores or made at home. These sheets are then filled with a blend of mashed potatoes, chopped onions, and spices like cumin and paprika. In addition to the potato filling, Algerian bourek may also include other variations such as tomatoes with minced meat, shrimp, chicken, or ground beef with cheese. The pastry is then folded into a triangular shape and either baked or deep fried until golden and crispy. Bourek comes in many different shapes and sizes, including triangles, rectangles, and spirals.

dish.shortDescription: Historically, burrito was a regional Mexican name for a taco, used in Guanajuato, Guerrero, Michoacán, San Luis Potosí, Sonora, and Sinaloa. Mexico City’s influence made “taco” the default; the name was forgotten.
dish.longDescription: The term burrito was regional, specifically from Guanajuato, Guerrero, Michoacán, San Luis Potosí, Sonora and Sinaloa, for what is known as a taco in Mexico City and surrounding areas, and codzito in Yucatán and Quintana Roo. Due to the cultural influence of Mexico City, the term taco became the default, and the meaning of terms like burrito and codzito were forgotten, leading many people to create new meanings and folk histories.

dish.longDescription: It is a ball-shaped bun containing pork or chicken meat, onions, eggs, mushrooms and vegetables. It often has Chinese sausage and a portion of a hard-boiled egg inside. They are filled with savory fillings, the most common being seasoned ground pork and quail egg. A vegetarian version also exists, containing a mix of mushrooms, tofu, glass noodles, and vegetables like carrots or jicama. Banh bao is a popular street food and is typically eaten as breakfast or a snack.

The main ingredient of this soup is beef, and it can be mixed with innards, such as intestine, liver, lungs, heart, tripe, or cow brain. The spices are used both for flavouring, and to balance the richness of the meat.

dish.shortDescription: An American fishcake of crab meat mixed with bread crumbs, mayonnaise, mustard, eggs, and seasonings, then sautéed, baked, grilled, deep-fried, or broiled. It is traditionally associated with Maryland’s Chesapeake Bay.
dish.longDescription: It is composed of crab meat and various other ingredients, such as bread crumbs, mayonnaise, mustard, eggs, and seasonings. It is then sautéed, baked, grilled, deep fried, or broiled. Crab cakes are traditionally associated with the Chesapeake Bay, in the state of Maryland. Although the earliest use of the term "crab cake" is commonly believed to date to Crosby Gaige's 1939 publication New York World's Fair Cook Book in which they are described as "Baltimore crab cakes," earlier usages can be found such as in Thomas J. Murrey's book Cookery with a Chafing Dish published in 1891.
dish.name: crab cake
dish.description: An American fishcake of crab meat mixed with bread crumbs, mayonnaise, mustard, eggs, and seasonings, then sautéed, baked, grilled, deep-fried, or broiled. It is traditionally associated with Maryland’s Chesapeake Bay.

dish.shortDescription: A Scottish dessert made to celebrate the August raspberry harvest, with cream, seasonal raspberries, Scottish oats, and whisky. Its roots lie in crowdie, a breakfast of cheese, toasted oatmeal, cream, and local honey.
dish.longDescription: It was originally a celebration of harvest, made following the raspberry harvest in August. The dessert of cream and fresh seasonal raspberries is bolstered by Scottish oats and whisky. It has been called "the uncontested king of Scottish desserts". Cranachan owes its origins to crowdie, a popular breakfast in which crowdie cheese is combined with lightly toasted oatmeal, cream, and local honey. Raspberries, when in season, might be added to the dish.

dish.shortDescription: A Japanese meat dish of chicken or pork with onion, carrot, potato, cabbage, and mixed vegetables, simmered in thick white roux. Milk may replace water for extra creaminess.
dish.longDescription: The vegetables are sauteed before the meat is added with some water. The surface fats are removed by degreasing, and then the roux is added. It is common in Japan to use ready-made roux, for making Japanese curry, which comes in a block from a box. The roux can also be cooked from scratch. The hard-paste roux melts from the heat and blends with the water to create a thick stew. Milk can also be used as a replacement for water to make the stew more creamy.

dish.shortDescription: A Chinese dish of freshwater shrimp immersed in liquor to make them easier to consume. Regional versions serve the shrimp raw, cook them in boiling water, or marinate cooked shrimp in rice wine.
dish.longDescription: The shrimp are immersed in liquor to make consumption easier, thus the name "drunken". Different parts of China have different recipes for the dish. For example, the shrimp are sometimes soaked in alcohol and then cooked in boiling water rather than served live, and in other recipes cooked shrimp are marinated in alcohol after they are boiled. Another version is based on shrimp that are submerged in a bowl of rice wine. The rice wine forces the shrimp to expel their wastes; the shrimp are then eaten, generally after their movement has ceased.

dish.shortDescription: A South Korean pork soup especially associated with Busan, made with soy sauce, miso, rice wine, sesame oil, and bone broth. Rice, kimchi, garlic, green peppers, and other sides can be added.
dish.longDescription: The name literally translates to "pork, soup, rice". It is served with various side dishes like rice, salted shrimp, onion, noodle, kimchi, garlic, and green peppers, which all can be added to the soup. It originated during the Korean War in the 1950s as poverty food. It eventually grew in popularity. The dish spread from Busan to the rest of the Gyeongsang province and eventually the rest of the country. However, the dish is not well-recognized outside of Korea. Busan has a street named after the dish, where there are dozens of restaurants that serve dwaeji-gukbap. These days it is often eaten while drinking liquor. It is also thought to be beneficial for women recovering from childbirth. The soup is enjoyed all year round and at any time of the day. Many establishments that serve the dish are open from morning to night, with some even open 24 hours.

dish.shortDescription: Indonesian curry-like beef soup from Cirebon, West Java, made with beef, intestine, tripe, and lungs cooked in coconut milk with garlic, chilies, chives, and sambal in a firewood-fired gentong stove.
dish.longDescription: It is a variety of the Soto cuisine and is similar to gulai which is usually cooked with firewood in a gentong stove. The ingredients include cuts of beef and cow offal such as intestine, tripes, lungs, etc. cooked with curry-like spices in coconut milk, garlic, chilies, chives (kuchai), and sambal in the form of chili powder. Empal gentong can be eaten with steamed rice, ketupat or lontong. It is originated in Battembat, Tengah Tani, and Cirebon Regency.

dish.shortDescription: An Indonesian iced fruit dessert of diced honeydew, cantaloupe, pineapple, papaya, squash, jackfruit, and kolang kaling mixed with ice and sweetened with sugar or syrup.
dish.longDescription: This cold and sweet beverage is made of diced fruits, such as honeydew, cantaloupe, pineapple, papaya, squash, jackfruit and kolang kaling, mixed with shaved ice or ice cubes, and sweetened with liquid sugar or syrup. The type of fruit used in this dessert may vary, some might add any available fruits such as mango, watermelon or longan — some imported fruits — such as lychee, kiwi, strawberry, pear, peach or grapes. Other ingredients might be added too, such as agar-agar jelly, grass jelly, seaweed or nata de coco. Some preparations also add basil seeds and use sweetened condensed milk or coconut milk in the liquid base.

dish.shortDescription: An Indonesian coconut-milk shaved-ice drink and dessert, a specialty of Bandung, West Java, with pink syrup, condensed milk, avocado, cassava tapai, ketan hitam tapai, jackfruit, diced bread, and pacar cina merah delima.
dish.longDescription: It is a specialty of Bandung, West Java. The main, or base, part is sugared sweet coconut milk-based ice in pink syrup, served with pacar cina merah delima, avocado, cassava tapai, ketan hitam tapai, jackfruit, diced bread and condensed milk. The condensed milk can be plain (white) or chocolate-flavoured. Es doger gains its pinkish color from rozen (rose) syrup, cocopandan syrup, or pink food coloring. Es doger is commonly sold by travelling vendor carts in major Indonesian cities, mainly in Bandung, Jakarta, Malang and Surabaya.

dish.longDescription: It is a traditional Christmas dish in the Italian provinces of Forlì-Cesena and Rimini, Emilia-Romagna, and in the Republic of San Marino. Ingredients include standard cake ingredients, such as flour, leavening, olive oil or shortening, sugar or honey, etc., along with cornmeal, breadcrumbs or stale bread, figs, raisins, diced apples, lemon rind and orange rind. Bustrengo is typically a dense and moist cake.

dish.shortDescription: A crown-shaped Corsican Easter cake made from yeast dough, with boiled eggs resembling bells inside its bell-tower form. The eggs signify renewed fertility after winter and recall bells released at Easter.
dish.longDescription: campanili) is a Corsican cake generally shaped like a crown, made of yeast dough. It is a typical dessert of the cuisine of Corsica and is a traditional Easter cake: the boiled eggs in the cake look like little bells inside the bell tower and represent the renewed fertility of the earth after the end of winter, remembering also the tradition to unleash the bells at Easter, after having tethered them at Good Friday.
dish.name: Campanile

dish.shortDescription: A thick, warm Mexican chocolate drink made with masa, corn flour, or masa harina, piloncillo, milk or water, and chocolate, then whisked with a molinillo; cinnamon, aniseed, vanilla, nuts, orange zest, or egg may be added.
dish.longDescription: It is prepared with either a masa, masa harina, or corn flour ; piloncillo; water or milk; chocolate; and occasionally cinnamon, aniseed, or vanilla. Ground nuts, orange zest, and egg can also be added to thicken and enrich the drink. Atole drinks are whipped up using a wooden whisk called a molinillo. The whisk is rolled between the palms of the hands, then moved back and forth in the mixture, until it is aerated and frothy; a blender may also be used.

dish.shortDescription: A South Indian lemon rice seasoned with mustard seeds, fried lentils, peanuts, curry leaves, chillies, lemon juice, and turmeric, with optional unripe mango and sometimes garlic and onions. It is a daily dish in Karnataka.
dish.longDescription: It is prepared by mixing cooked rice with a special seasoning called Oggarane or Gojju. Characteristic of the seasoning are mustard seeds, fried lentils, peanuts, curry leaves, chillies, lemon juice and other optional items such as scrapes of unripe mango. Added turmeric powder gives Chitranna its yellow color. Garlic and onions are also used in the seasoning by some, although traditionally they do not form part of the recipe. The dish is especially popular in the south Indian state of Karnataka, where it has become a part of the daily diet.

dish.shortDescription: A traditional Christmas Eve dish in Central Europe, with carp kept in a bathtub to remove muddy flavours before being fried or served as gefilte fish.
dish.longDescription: The fish is traditionally kept in a bathtub before preparation to remove muddy flavours and is commonly fried or served in dishes like gefilte fish. In some regions, leftover bones are placed in fruit trees for spring growth and its scales are carried for good luck. Some beliefs link its head to Christ's torture instruments and protection against witches.
dish.name: Christmas carp
dish.description: A traditional Christmas Eve dish in Central Europe, with carp kept in a bathtub to remove muddy flavours before being fried or served as gefilte fish.

dish.shortDescription: An Andean soup or stew from the mountains of South America, made in large portions for marketplaces and events and sometimes served with wine as a warming food in the cold climate.
dish.longDescription: Chupe Andino may be prepared by Andean people, those that live in the region. It is sometimes prepared in large portions to feed many people at marketplaces and events. Chupe Andino is sometimes served with wine as an accompaniment. Soups and stews play a significant part in Andean cuisine, because the cold weather in the region demands nutritious, fatty foods that are warming.
dish.name: Chupe Andino
dish.description: An Andean soup or stew from the mountains of South America, made in large portions for marketplaces and events and sometimes served with wine as a warming food in the cold climate.

dish.shortDescription: An Italian ring-shaped cake with regional variations. A basic version combines flour, baking powder, salt, eggs, milk, sugar, oil, and vanilla, with honey sometimes added; the sugar and eggs are whisked before baking in a ring-shaped pan.
dish.longDescription: As an example, a basic version of the cake could be prepared using flour, baking powder, salt, eggs, milk, sugar, oil, and vanilla flavouring. Honey is sometimes added as a sweetener. To create the light texture the sugar and eggs are whisked together, and oil and milk are added while whisking continuously until the mixture is frothy. Then sifted baking powder and flour are added to the dry ingredients and the cake is baked in a ring shaped pan.
dish.name: Ciambella PAT
dish.description: An Italian ring-shaped cake with regional variations. A basic version combines flour, baking powder, salt, eggs, milk, sugar, oil, and vanilla, with honey sometimes added; the sugar and eggs are whisked before baking in a ring-shaped pan.

dish.longDescription: A later technique for clarification employs gelatin filtration. Consommés are most commonly made from beef or veal, but chicken, fish and game variants are recognised in French cuisine. They may be served on their own – hot or chilled – or be used as the basis of many soups, sauces and stews.

dish.shortDescription: Filipino spaghetti adapts Italian spaghetti with a sweet Bolognese sauce: tomato sauce sweetened with brown sugar, banana ketchup, or condensed milk. It is topped with hot dogs or longganisa, giniling, and grated cheese.
dish.longDescription: It has a distinctively sweet sauce, usually made from tomato sauce sweetened with brown sugar, banana ketchup, or condensed milk. It is typically topped with sliced hot dogs or smoked longganisa sausages, giniling, and grated cheese. It is regarded as a comfort food in Philippine cuisine. dish.shortDescription: A savory breakfast from Tianjin, China, Guoba cuisine has vegetarian and meat varieties, though the vegetarian version remains most popular.
dish.longDescription: Although its origin is unknown, it is thought to have a history spanning over 300 years. Guoba cuisine is known for its pleasantly-salty taste. It was divided into two varieties, vegetarian and meat, but only the vegetarian version is still popular. Dafulai Guoba Cuisine is the most iconic and long-lasting brand of Guoba dishes in Tianjin. In 1997, Dafulai Guoba cuisine was ranked among the first batch of "Famous Chinese Snacks" by the Chinese Cooking Association. In 2009, its cooking techniques were added to the intangible cultural heritage of Tianjin. Guoba cuisine is most popular in Tianjin, but can also be found in Tianjin restaurants in Chinese communities across the U.S. and Canada.

dish.shortDescription: A Spanish bread from Galicia made with native soft wheat flour, other wheat flour, water, sourdough, yeast, and salt. Its high hydration and long fermentation create an airy, slightly acidic crumb beneath a crisp, golden-brown crust.
dish.longDescription: It contains soft wheat flour native to Galicia, called "trigo do país", mixed with foreign wheat flour, traditionally from Castille, in addition to water, sourdough, yeast and salt. It is characterized by high hydration, which gives it a spongy crumb with abundant irregular pores and a pale cream to dark white color. In addition, it has an intense and slightly acidic flavor, thanks to a prolonged fermentation time. Its crust is floured, aromatic, very crisp, and golden to dark brown in color.

dish.shortDescription: A Piedmont chocolate shaped like an ingot and wrapped in gold or silver foil, a Turin specialty named for the gianduja blend of chocolate and hazelnut.
dish.longDescription: Gianduiotti are shaped like ingots and individually wrapped in a (usually) gold- or silver-colored foil cover. They are a specialty of Turin, and take their name from gianduja, the blend of chocolate and hazelnut used for gianduiotti and other sweets, including Nutella. This blend itself is named after Gianduja, a mask in commedia dell'arte, a type of Italian theater, that represents the Piemonte. Gianduja's tricorner hat inspired the shape of the gianduiotto.
dish.name: Giandujotto PAT
dish.description: A Piedmont chocolate shaped like an ingot and wrapped in gold or silver foil, a Turin specialty named for the gianduja blend of chocolate and hazelnut.

dish.longDescription: It also includes different kinds of sauces, usually chilli, garlic, and barbecue. Yoghurt or yoghurt sauce, cheese, jalapeño peppers, and tabbouleh are also common additions. The snack pack has been described as a staple takeaway dish of kebab shops in Australia.

dish.shortDescription: A white surimi product from Japan with a soft, mild taste, made in square, triangular, or round forms. Believed to have been created by Hanpei of Suruga during the Edo period, it is used in oden, soups, and stews, or fried and broiled.
dish.longDescription: It is believed to have been invented during the Edo period in Japan by a chef, Hanpei (半平) of Suruga, and the dish is named after him. Another theory suggests that because it is triangle shaped and appears to have been cut in half from a square, it is a half  piece . It can be eaten as an ingredient in oden or other Japanese soups and stews. It can also be fried or broiled.

dish.shortDescription: A South African vegetable relish, usually spicy, served with bread, pap, samp, stews, or curries. It reportedly developed among Mozambican mineworkers near Johannesburg from tinned produce with chili in a Portuguese style.
dish.longDescription: Chakalaka is said to have originated in the townships of Johannesburg or in the gold mines surrounding Johannesburg, when Mozambican mineworkers leaving their shift cooked tinned produce with chili to produce a spicy Portuguese-style relish to accompany pap. Many variations of Chakalaka exist, depending on region and family tradition. Some versions include beans, cabbage and butternut squash. For example, canned baked beans, canned tomatoes, onion, garlic, and curry paste can be used to make the dish.

dish.shortDescription: A Japanese savoury egg custard seasoned with soy sauce, dashi and mirin, with shiitake, kamaboko, yuri-ne, ginkgo and boiled shrimp in a tea-cup-like container, eaten with a spoon.
dish.longDescription: Unlike many other custards, it is usually eaten as a dish in a meal, as chawanmushi contains savory rather than sweet ingredients. The custard consists of an egg mixture seasoned with soy sauce, dashi, and mirin, with numerous ingredients such as shiitake mushrooms, kamaboko, yuri-ne, ginkgo and boiled shrimp placed into a tea-cup-like container. The recipe for the dish is similar to that of Chinese steamed eggs, but the toppings often differ. Since egg custards cannot be picked up by chopsticks, it is one of the few Japanese dishes that are eaten with a spoon.

dish.shortDescription: A Hanoi grilled-fish delicacy: hemibagrus catfish marinated with turmeric, galangal, and fermented rice, then charcoal-grilled and eaten with scallion, dill, bún noodles, herbs, peanuts, and mắm tôm.
dish.longDescription: The dish is traditionally made with hemibagrus, which is a genus of catfish. The fish is cut into pieces and marinated with turmeric, galangal, fermented rice and other ingredients. It is then grilled over charcoal and served at the table in a hot pan coated with oil with scallion and dill. It is then eaten with bún noodles, fresh herbs, peanuts and a pungent shrimp-based sauce called mắm tôm. Chả Cá Lá Vọng is considered a Hanoi delicacy, as it is nearly exclusively served in restaurants and is not found in street food.
dish.name: chả cá Lã Vọng
dish.description: A Hanoi grilled-fish delicacy: hemibagrus catfish marinated with turmeric, galangal, and fermented rice, then charcoal-grilled and eaten with scallion, dill, bún noodles, herbs, peanuts, and mắm tôm.

dish.shortDescription: Vietnamese green rice made by roasting young kernels over low heat, then pounding them flat. Chewy and slightly sweet with a nutty taste, it is eaten plain or with coconut shavings and is popular in the Red River Delta.
dish.longDescription: It is not dyed green, but produced from young rice kernels roasted over very low heat then pounded in a mortar and pestle until flattened. Cốm is a seasonal dish associated with autumn. It can be eaten plain or with coconut shavings. The taste is slightly sweet with a nutty flavor. It is a popular seasonal dessert across Vietnam, especially in Red River Delta cuisine. It is traditionally produced at the Cốm Vòng village in Hanoi.
dish.name: cốm

dish.shortDescription: A Brazilian grain of toasted cassava meal, usually seasoned with salt, smoked meat, and spices. It ranges from coarse grains to fine powder and adds smoky, salty flavor to barbecued meat and hearty stews.
dish.longDescription: It is eaten mainly in Brazil. It can be found commercially produced and packaged but can also be prepared at home based on family recipes. Most recipes also contain some salt, smoked meat, and spices. The consistency of the mixture ranges from large grains the size of cracked bulgur wheat or couscous down to a table-salt-sized powder. Most farofas have a very smoky and slightly salty taste, by and large used to accentuate the taste of meat, particularly barbecued meat and hearty stews.
dish.name: farofa

Some cooks may choose to fry rather than toast to avoid having to give counter or storage space to or spend money on a toaster. Proponents of frying rather than toasting call out the extra flavor and crispiness that can be achieved by frying in fat rather than dry-toasting.

dish.shortDescription: A Chinese rice dish made by stir-frying cooked rice in a wok or frying pan, usually with eggs, vegetables, seafood, or meat. It developed during the Sui dynasty and spread through Chinese migration.
dish.longDescription: It is often eaten as a main dish or as an accompaniment to another dish. Fried rice is a popular component of East Asian, Southeast Asian, South Asian and American Chinese cuisines. As a homemade dish, fried rice is typically made with ingredients left over from other dishes, leading to countless variations. Fried rice first developed during the Sui dynasty in China and later spread across the world through the migration of the Chinese diaspora.

dish.description: A Chinese rice dish made by stir-frying cooked rice in a wok or frying pan, usually with eggs, vegetables, seafood, or meat. It developed during the Sui dynasty and spread through Chinese migration.

dish.shortDescription: A French dish of boned meat, usually poultry or fish, stuffed with forcemeat, pressed into a cylinder, poached, and served cold, often coated with aspic and lavishly decorated.
dish.longDescription: Galantines are often stuffed with forcemeat, and pressed into a cylindrical shape. Since boning poultry can be difficult and time-consuming for the novice, this is a rather elaborate dish, which is often lavishly decorated, hence its name, connoting a presentation at table that is galant, or urbane and sophisticated. In the later nineteenth century the technique's origin was already attributed to the chef of the marquis de Brancas.
